articles.title: Aaron Judge's Updated Injury Status for Yankees vs. Rays in 2026 MLB Playoffs
articles.summary: The New York Yankees will be without Aaron Judge for their ALDS matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees will be without Aaron Judge for their ALDS matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays.

New York confirmed Judge's absence ahead of Game 1 after Jack Curry of YES first reported his absence.

Judge initially said he hoped to return for the beginning of the postseason before he was left off the Yankees' Wild Card roster amid his recovery from the right calf strain that resulted in a trip to the injured list on Sept. 19.

Yankees manager Aaron Boone said at the time the decision was made because the club didn't feel Judge was "all the way back."

Judge has appeared in just seven games for the Yankees since he was shut down with a right rib injury May 31. Following his return Sept. 8, he was held to a batting average of .174 with one home run in 24 plate appearances before suffering the calf injury.

The Yankees will hope giving Judge more time to recover from his latest injury will result in a more productive return from the slugger. With Judge sitting out the divisional series, he will gain an additional week to recover in the event the Yankees advance to the ALCS.

Gerrit Cole will start Game 1 for the Yankees when the ALDS begins Saturday at 6:30 p.m. ET in St. Petersburg. He will be facing a more rested lineup given that the Rays sat out the Wild Card round after clinching the AL's top seed.

articles.title: Braves' bats and 100-degree heat prove no problem for Tarik Skubal in Dodgers' decisive NLDS Game 1 win
articles.summary: "I played a Little League game in 127," the lefty claimed after L.A.'s 5-3 victory.
articles.body:
LOS ANGELES — The radar gun said 98.4. The thermometer said 100. Heat, everywhere you looked.

On Saturday, for the first time in his big-league career, Tarik Skubal started a ballgame with a fastball that clocked in below the first-pitch temperature. One inning later, he bested the sultry conditions with a 101.1-mph heater. Neither the weather nor the Atlanta Braves were a match for the two-time Cy Young Award winner.

Skubal conquered them both in NLDS Game 1, tossing a gem to lead the two-time defending champs to a rousing 5-3 victory . Beneath a cruel sun and a cloudless sky, Skubal, the trade deadline headliner, stole the show in his first postseason start as a Dodger. The hottest MLB postseason game since Game 1 of the 2017 World Series was a fitting environment for a guy who grew up on the fringes of the Mojave Desert. Rocking three-quarter-length sleeves, the towering southpaw looked entirely unaffected by the triple-digit heat.

"I thought Tarik was fantastic. I thought the fastball was really good ..." Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said afterward. "Obviously, probably the hottest game he's pitched in."

Slow down there, skip. Skubal, who grew up in Kingman, Arizona, said during his postgame news conference that he played in even harsher conditions as a kid.

"I played a Little League game in 127," the Dodgers lefty claimed. "Lake Havasu."

Temperature logs from the biggest city in Mohave County, Arizona, tell a slightly different story. The steamiest day on record that overlaps with Skubal's Little League tenure was a comparatively frosty 124-degree afternoon on June 20, 2008. But details aside, that boiling day 18 years ago in Lake Havasu stuck in Skubal's mind for a reason: It ain't easy pitching in a convection oven.

"I always say the best way to combat weather, if it's cold or hot, is to have quick innings and get your guys back on the field hitting and getting off the mound," he said.

Good thing, then, that Skubal spent more of his afternoon relaxing between innings in the Dodgers' clubhouse than he did boiling in the sun. After allowing a single to the first batter of the game, Atlanta DH Drake Baldwin, the 6-foot-3, 240-pound hurler retired the next 15 Braves. As often happens with starters in the October pressure-cooker, Skubal's fastball velocity jumped a full mile per hour above its season average. That allowed his dastardly changeup to be even more effective, conjuring eight whiffs on 15 swings.

Those five untouchable innings were a resounding reminder of why the former Detroit Tiger dominated the discourse around this year's trade deadline. No starting pitcher is an automatic win, but Skubal might be as close as it comes. He finished the day with seven strikeouts across six innings, with Sean Murphy's solo crank in the sixth the only blotch on an otherwise decisive showing.

That swing from the Atlanta backstop, which cut LA's lead to 2-1, offered the Braves their only opportunity to turn a waltz into a contest. Skubal oh so briefly wavered, walking the nine-hitter, Ha-Seong Kim, before collecting a pair of outs on fielder's choices. Another free pass to Ozzie Albies followed, and the Braves had the tying run on second and the go-ahead run on first with two outs.

The game tightened. Skubal's pitch count rounded 90. All-Star slugger Matt Olson strode to the plate. Pitching coach Mark Prior sauntered to the mound for a visit. Down in the bullpen, reliever Alex Vesia readied himself to enter the fray. More than 50,000 sweaty and sunburned souls rose to their feet.

Then Skubal, of course, rose to the occasion.

Olson flied out harmlessly to left field on a 99.7-mph fastball a few inches off the plate. Skubal hollered and pumped his fist into his glove as he strode back toward a welcoming Dodgers dugout. His day was done. Only then did the 29-year-old soon-to-be free agent realize just how unrelentingly warm it was.

"I didn't really think it was that hot out there until I got done and I walked back in the dugout, and I asked — I forget who was sitting, I think it was [Blake] Snell — I was like, 'Has it been this hot all game?'" he said afterward.

Atlanta starter Dylan Dodd, an Illinois-raised lefty, didn't wilt in the conditions, either. Dodd was a silver lining for the Braves, tossing three scoreless innings in his first MLB start since 2023. Skubal, for comparison, has made 100 starts in that time. In fact, Dodd's most recent start at any level was a Sept. 19, 2024, outing for the Triple-A Gwinnett Stripers against the Jacksonville Jumbo Shrimp.

Even so, Dodd traded punches with Skubal until the Braves lefty ran out of pitches. Then Atlanta skipper Walt Weiss went to Victor Mederos to start the fourth. Teoscar Hernández greeted the new arm with a two-run long ball to put the Dodgers on the board, a blast that included one of the farthest-flung bat flips you'll ever see .

Kyle Tucker clobbered a two-run shot right after Skubal's departure to put the Dodgers up three. Max Muncy added a solo blast later in the frame. Atlanta would claw back in the ninth with an Ozzie Albies two-run homer off Tanner Scott, eventually bringing the tying run to the plate. But Evan Phillips ended things by getting a lazy bouncer off Austin Riley's bat.

An understandably exhausted and dehydrated crowd roared one last time. On Sunday, some of them will return to watch another two-time Cy Young Award winner, Snell, try to silence Atlanta's bats once again. Such is the absurdity of LA's rotation. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, last October's grand hero, won't throw until Game 3. Skubal might not need to pitch again in this series.

As the victorious Dodgers flooded the field for ceremonial high-fives and handshakes with towels covering their necks, a graphic reading "10 more wins" blinked across the stadium jumbotrons. For any other franchise, that sentiment might come across as aspirational. For the Dodgers, it feels like a statement of intent.

October in Los Angeles has begun, and it gets only hotter from here.

articles.title: Home rail advantage? Padres lose possible go-ahead HR in NLDS when ball hits ceiling at Brewers' American Family Field
articles.summary: The Padres weren't happy with how the Brewers got the second out of the ninth inning.
articles.body:
Ty France thought he had that one. The ceiling of the Milwaukee Brewers' American Family Field begged to differ.

A dramatic Game 1 of the NLDS came down to the ninth inning Saturday , with the Brewers leading 3-2 and closer Trevor Megill going for a four-out save against the San Diego Padres. With one out and a man on, France blasted a fly ball that went high and deep — but then a little too high.

The ball bounced off a railing in the roof and fell harmlessly into the glove of Brewers left fielder Jackson Chourio for the second out. France clearly believed he deserved more, and so did his team, as Padres manager Craig Stammen challenged the call on the field.

A replay review upheld the call, ruling that the ball was live and fair.

The Fox Sports broadcast speculated that the ball could be turned into a go-ahead homer, but no such provision exists in the American Family Field ground rules . There are such provisions in other parks, such as the Tampa Bay Rays' Tropicana Field , but the American Family Field rules decide only whether a ball is fair or foul:

Batted ball striking roof, roof truss or roof cable over fair territory: In Play If caught by fielder, batter is out and runners advance at own risk. Batted ball striking roof, roof truss or roof cable over foul territory: Dead Ball

Batted ball striking roof, roof truss or roof cable over fair territory: In Play

If caught by fielder, batter is out and runners advance at own risk.

Batted ball striking roof, roof truss or roof cable over foul territory: Dead Ball

That's what was being reviewed, whether the ball was fair or foul, and the replay booth decided the ball struck the roof over fair territory. France wasn't happy with the call, but winning the challenge would have merely made it a 1-1 count, not a two-run homer.

This was apparently something Stammen discussed with the umpires before the game, as he told reporters later :

"We joked about it at the umpire meeting today, about what would happen if the ball hit the roof. It was unlikely, but it happened. The rule is if they deem the ball to be fair and it comes down, you can catch it. If it hits off the roof foul, it's a foul ball. They ruled that it hit the roof fair and the outfielder caught it. "Unfortunately, it's a bad break for us. It looked like it was a possible home run. Just didn't go our way."

"We joked about it at the umpire meeting today, about what would happen if the ball hit the roof. It was unlikely, but it happened. The rule is if they deem the ball to be fair and it comes down, you can catch it. If it hits off the roof foul, it's a foul ball. They ruled that it hit the roof fair and the outfielder caught it.

"Unfortunately, it's a bad break for us. It looked like it was a possible home run. Just didn't go our way."

The real debate was whether France's fly ball would have been a homer with an open roof. MLB.com's AJ Cassavell reported that there was a postgame consensus that the ball was probably gone in an open air park. That included Brewers manager Pat Murphy, who chalked it up to intervention from late Brewers legend Bob Uecker :

"Ueck decided to put a hand on it," he said.

But that might not be so, if MLB's numbers are right. According to Statcast, France hit the ball with a 105.3-mph exit velocity and a 49-degree launch angle. Those are the numbers of a hard-hit ball hit perhaps a bit too high.

France had every reason to think he crushed that ball. Megill did, too, as he said after the game that his reaction was " Oh, crap. " However, it might be a stretch to say that the Padres were clearly robbed based on the currently available data. Consider that batters had a .038 batting average on balls with launch angles of 49 degrees this season .

That does seem to conflict with the eye test, though, as Chourio caught the ball at the warning track and the ball did seem to lose distance with the contact.

France made a case for a change to the ground rules that would have allowed him to avoid an out:

"With all the technology and data we have now ... there should be something put in place right there," France said. "That shouldn't be an out."

Of course, none of us knows this stuff for sure. That's the real frustration of the ball hitting that railing — that the game was decided by steel instead of wood and leather. Either way, it was one final piece of drama in an eventful game.

San Diego will take that disappointment into Game 2, scheduled for 4 p.m. ET Sunday in Milwaukee.

articles.title: No, the San Diego Padres didn't lose because of controversial ninth inning home run ruling
articles.summary: Major League Baseball's Statcast exit velocity and launch angle data reveal why Ty France's controversial roof ball was not the home run he believed.
articles.body: If there's one thing the Major League Baseball postseason always delivers, it's drama. And Saturday night's game between the San Diego Padres and Milwaukee Brewers certainly had more than its fair share. The Brewers entered the game and the series as big favorites, thanks in large part to likely NL Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski starting game one. Misiorowski has been nearly unhittable this season, with a minuscule 1.80 ERA, just 96 hits allowed all season, and 252 strikeouts in 174.2 innings. But the Padres have been baseball's hottest team down the stretch, and were able to force him out after pushing across two runs in just four innings. But the Brewers battled back, tying the game on a Jackson Chourio homer and taking the lead late on another from William Contreras. The Padres missed an opportunity in the top of the 8th, but started the 9th with the heart of their lineup facing closer Trevor Megill. Dustin Harris singled to lead off the ninth, Manny Machado struck out, and Ty France launched what's now become one of the most controversial fly balls in recent postseason history. BREWERS TAKE GAME 1 OF NLDS AFTER A CONTROVERSIAL CALL ON SURE-FIRE HOME RUN BALL THAT HIT THE STADIUM ROOF While it looked at first glance like a potential go-ahead home run, or might fly harmlessly foul, France hit the ball so high it banged off the roof support system at American Family Field and fell into the field of play just onto the warning track in left field, where Jackson Chourio caught it for an out. Several minutes of discussion followed, with the umpires ruling on the field that it was, in fact, a fair ball and effectively a fly ball out. Many fans, and some of the players, were clearly confused, assuming that a ball hitting the roof would become immediately "dead" and the play restarted. By rule though, there's no question that the umpires made the correct call. Major League Baseball's ground rule page, specifically covering American Family Field, covers this exact situation. If the "Batted ball strikes roof, roof truss, roof cable, or any cabling over fair territory," the rule states, it's considered "In Play." "If caught by fielder," it continues, "batter is out, and runners advance at own risk." That's exactly what was determined on the field, and what the replay review confirmed. The ball was in fair territory when it hit the roof, it fell down to the field of play where it was caught by an outfielder, and the hitter is out. Controversy over, right? Well, not exactly. Many fans, obviously most notably Padres fans, are convinced that the ball would have been a home run had it not hit the roof. France himself said as much after the game in the clubhouse. "You would think with all the technology we have now we’d be able to make a clear call on that," France said. "There should be something put in place right there. That shouldn’t be an out. … We’ve got ball tracking. We’ve got exit velo. We’ve got projected distances. We have all that stuff." And that's where the second part of the controversy has continued, and even grown. Had the ball not hit the roof, would it have been a game, and potentially series, changing home run? France is right; we do have ball tracking, exit velocity and projected distances, thanks to the league's Statcast operation. And those metrics all but confirmed one thing: that was not going to be a home run. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Statcast measured France's fly ball at 105.3mph exit velocity at a whopping 49 degree launch angle. The projected distance? 325 feet. The wall in Milwaukee? Well, it's hard to know exactly where the ball would have come down if unobstructed, but the shortest dimension is 342 feet directly at the foul pole. Had the ball been more towards left center, it's even further. There's more to it than that. Statcast predicted "expected" batting average, essentially how often balls hit with those exact characteristics become hits, was .050. Balls hit 105.3mph at 49 degrees are outs 99.5% of the time. They're also home runs in just one stadium: Daikin Park in Houston, thanks to the short porch with the Crawford Boxes. Thanks to Statcast, we can compare similarly hit baseballs with that exact launch angle and see the results. Here's the list from 2026: THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Expanding the search to 2024 and 2025, there were a number of other balls that met these exact characteristics. Of the 15 batted ball events, including 2026, 14 were outs, with one double from Aaron Judge in 2024. The furthest a batted ball traveled with those exact numbers was 337 feet, a fly ball from Cody Bellinger in April 2025. There are different outcomes because of weather conditions, the exact backspin of the ball, and many other variables. But with the exact measurements available to us, not a single ball hit with that velocity and launch angle traveled far enough to cover the left field wall at American Family Field, even if it were directly down the line. France, though, was convinced it was "going out." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER "I guess the biggest question was whether it was going to stay fair or foul," he said. "I thought I backspun it and thought it was going to stay fair. Knew it was going out." Players aren't reliable narrators when it comes to judging distance. Data is. And the data shows France's fly ball wouldn't have cleared the fence. Fluky and bizarre and open to endless debate? Yes. Postseason robbery? No.

articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers grabbed a 2-0 series lead against the San Diego Padres in epic fashion on Sunday night.

The Milwaukee Brewers grabbed a 2-0 series lead against the San Diego Padres in epic fashion on Sunday night.

Trailing by a run in the bottom of the ninth, Jackson Chourio was at the plate in a bases-loaded situation with two outs. After a two-strike foul, Chourio drilled one up the middle to bring in both the tying and the winning run.

The Padres got on the board early when Ty France drove in a run in the top of the first, and San Diego made it 2-0 in the fifth inning on a fielder's choice. The Brewers finally got on the board in the bottom of the fifth when Sal Frelick drove in Christian Yelich.

France gave the Padres a cushion in the top of the seventh with an RBI single, but Milwaukee cut the lead back down to one run when the Brewers scored on an error.

After keeping San Diego off the board in the top of the ninth, the Brewers had one last chance to force extras or win the game.

Yelich drew a one-out walk and stole second before Frelick was walked. Gary Sánchez then drew a two-out walk to load the bases for Chourio, and the 22-year-old delivered the walk-off on the sixth pitch of the at-bat.

After swinging the momentum of the series with an exciting win, the Brewers will head to San Diego for Game 3 on Tuesday.

Instead of going to another reliever to get the final out, manager Craig Stammen left him in to face Chourio. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER It didn't work. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD On a 2-2 pitch, Chourio crushed a liner 109.5mph to center, driving in Yelich and Frelick for a stunning 4-3 walk-off win and 2-0 series lead. Miller blew just three saves in the regular season and allowed just 37 total hits. But he faced nine hitters on Sunday, far more than a typical outing. While his velocity never really dipped, three walks showed he was not as sharp as he typically is. It's understandable Stammen wanted to live and die with the best relief pitcher in baseball instead of risking it with someone like Jason Adam or David Morgan. But at 34 pitches, facing the best hitter Milwaukee has, having already walked three hitters, it's reasonable to wonder if the Padres would have been better served by making a pitching change. Regardless, it's too late now. The Brewers have won back-to-back one-run games against a team that typically excels at winning them. They beat Mason Miller, which for most of the year seemed all but impossible. They've ensured that the worst case scenario to win the series is a return to Milwaukee for a game 5 started by Jacob Misiorowski. The Padres, with their season on the line, will send Nick Pivetta to the mound in San Diego on Tuesday night to try and extend it to game four. The Brewers will counter with Dustin May, hoping to finish out the sweep and give themselves another break before the NLCS. Perhaps the only good news for the Padres? Petco Park has no roof to worry about.

articles.title: Down to their last strike, Jackson Chourio and the Brewers find a way in NLDS Game 2: 'One of my favorite games I've been a part of'
articles.summary: The fans in Milwaukee didn't have a whole lot to cheer about for 8 2/3 innings. Then Chourio delivered.
articles.body:
MILWAUKEE — More than 41,000 Brewers fans had little to celebrate going into the ninth inning of Game 2 of the NLDS on Sunday. They were probably frustrated most of the game. For eight innings, their Brewers had looked unrecognizable. Eight innings of sloppy baseball, including three errors and two unearned runs, combined with a lack of offense had the Brewers on the brink of losing their first game of this postseason to the San Diego Padres. And against MLB's best and most intimidating closer, Mason Miller, things looked grim.

Then the Brewers remembered who they are. It might've taken 8 2/3 innings, but in their 4-3 walk-off victory over the Padres in Game 2 , they gave a sellout crowd at American Family Field a reason to cheer and a game they'll never forget.

"One of my favorite games I've been a part of," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. "And what's most gratifying to see is how many of our great fans came out to see that one. Just happy for the club, happy for the city that they got to witness something so special."

But let's back up. Before Milwaukee could attempt to walk off San Diego, it first had to tie the game against Miller after entering the ninth down 3-2. And that required baserunners, which Miller didn't yield in the eighth inning when he first appeared in Sunday's game. San Diego had allowed very little traffic, and the Brewers had mustered just four hits prior to the ninth. Newly minted Brewers captain Christian Yelich worked a five-pitch walk against Miller to put the tying run on first base with one out.

Of course, one at-bat doesn't make for a comeback against the game's best reliever. But for a team like the Brewers, who have always believed as an organization that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, the mindset was to keep the line moving.

"Just grind, man. Just find a way to get on there," Yelich said afterward. "Doesn't matter if it's a walk or a hit. We just want some traffic in that inning there, and just see what happens."

Yelich handed the baton to Sal Frelick, who fell behind in the count 1-2, a place no hitter wants to be. But then the Brewers' right fielder buckled down, taking three straight Miller pitches to draw another walk.

"Guys like that don't give up multiple hits in innings very often," Frelick said. "He was tasked with six outs today, so wanted to kind of get pressure on him, see if we could get some guys on."

Following an Andrew Vaughn flyout for the second out, arguably the biggest at-bat of the ninth came from catcher Gary Sánchez, who pinch hit for David Hamilton. Sánchez is on the Brewers' NLDS roster for moments like this — opportunities for a big swing. Just like his teammates, the veteran wasn't necessarily looking for a three-run shot.

Like Yelich and Frelick before him, Sánchez was able to grind and put together another tough at-bat against Miller. After working the count full, he drew the Brewers' third walk of the inning.

"He's the best in the game," first baseman Jake Bauers said of Miller before the series. "I think the mentality is try to have a good at-bat. Whatever happens after that is whatever happens."

What happened is Milwaukee's biggest star came up in the biggest moment. With the bases loaded and two out in the bottom of the ninth, who else would step into the box but Jackson Chourio?

Having announced his presence in this series with a game-tying, two-run shot in the Brewers' Game 1 victory , Chourio had plenty of confidence going into his at-bat against Miller. And the 22-year-old wasn't trying to play here. He understood exactly what was unfolding.

"Watching those at-bats beforehand, I knew that he was a little bit erratic," Chourio said of Miller. "He was throwing some balls. I knew that he was gonna come at me with the fastball at some point, so mentally, I was just making sure that I was prepared for that."

The first two times Miller came at Chourio with the fastball, it worked; Chourio swung-and-missed at 100.8 mph and 102.2 mph before fouling off 103.5 mph. But after taking a tough slider to make it a 2-2 count, Chourio decided to call game.

Miller offered a 101.3 mph fastball, and Chourio ripped a 109.5 mph single into center field, past a diving Jake Cronenworth. Yelich scored easily from third, and as a flying Frelick slid across home plate to beat the throw from center fielder Jackson Merrill, the crowd let out a collective roar.

"I think it's probably in the top three of the special moments I've had in my career," Chourio said afterward.

Since he made his major league debut at just 20 years old, the Brewers have known that Chourio is special. After his first three seasons in the big leagues, with him already having monster postseason numbers, that bar might not be high enough.

"I think he's been that type of player. The talent is undeniable when you watch him play," Yelich said of Chourio. "There's nothing he can't do on the baseball field. The more experience he gets, the more situations he's in, the more he kind of learns the league and just racks up the at-bats, he's just going to continue to get better.

"And that's kind of scary because he's pretty good right now."

Said Murphy: "He's starting to realize how he has to play the game. As talented as he is, he's still learning the game. … As a hitter, when he stays under control, it's amazing. He's, I think, turning into a bona fide, top-flight player. Couldn't be happier for him because he brings it every day."

With Chourio's heroics, the Brewers take a commanding 2-0 NLDS lead on the Padres and will head to San Diego one win away from returning to the NLCS. By winning a game Sunday in which they didn't play anywhere close to their best until the very end, the Brewers showed that they can find a way no matter what.

"It's the attention to detail that is instilled in our culture, stuff that I learned from [Yelich] when I first got called up," Frelick said. "If you're not doing it, you don't play."

"It's a team that's unified," Chourio said. "We know what our strengths are, and we know how to support each other. … Everyone's supporting each other, and we know how to win."

articles.title: Braves Beat Dodgers to Even NLDS, Box Score Stats, Highlights, Updated MLB Playoff Bracket
articles.summary: The Atlanta Braves evened things up in the National League Division Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday.
articles.body:
The Atlanta Braves evened things up in the National League Division Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday.

On a relatively slow offensive night, the Braves used a shutdown performance from Didier Fuentes out of the bullpen to take down the Dodgers 3-2.

MLB playoff game among hottest ever in history

Mauricio Dubón got things started for Atlanta, driving in Ronald Acuña Jr. on an infield single in the top of the first inning. The Dodgers answered the Braves' run in the fourth inning when Freddie Freeman hit a solo shot.

The Braves regained the lead in the top of the fifth when Michael Harris II scored on a wild pitch, and Harris then drove in Matt Olson to make it 3-1 in the seventh inning.

Fuentes was perhaps the biggest hero of the night. The 21-year-old is playing in the postseason for the first time this year, but he looked like a veteran when he faced Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts and other stars.

Fuentes came in to start the sixth inning and sat down 11 straight batters before giving up a solo home run to Max Muncy in the bottom of the ninth. With Fuentes picking up the first two outs of the inning, the veteran closer, Raisel Iglesias, came in to record the final out.

The Braves are hoping to end the back-to-back champions' season in the divisional round, and more strong defensive performances like the one on Sunday will get the job done.

The series will head to Atlanta for Game 3 on Tuesday.

articles.title: Atlanta Braves, led by surprise hero Didier Fuentes, cobble together bullpen game victory in NLDS Game 2: 'It's stuff you would never do in the regular season'
articles.summary: Six Braves pitchers held the Dodgers to two runs as Atlanta evened the series 1-1.
articles.body:
LOS ANGELES — As Didier Fuentes crossed himself and thanked the heavens, his bosses on Earth convened to discuss his fate.

The 21-year-old, baby-faced Colombian was a man — a kid, actually — in total flow state. He'd just retired the side in the eighth, his third consecutive perfect inning against the two-time defending champs. After he entered to start the sixth, it'd been nine up, nine down, thank you very much. Los Angeles' imposing lineup full of MVPs and All-Stars and October-familiar veterans looked utterly lost against the rookie right-hander in this knife's-edge NLDS Game 2 .

As Fuentes strolled off the mound beneath a scared-silent Dodger Stadium, with his club clinging to a 3-1 lead, three measly outs stood between the Braves and an even series.

But who exactly would be trusted to collect those outs?

Manager Walt Weiss and his brain trust — a six-man think tank of ballcoaches who'd spent the night navigating a most complicated bullpen game — huddled to discuss the decision. They could either stick with the cruising Fuentes or hand the ball to closer Raisel Iglesias, warm and ready in the Braves' bullpen. Fuentes had thrown three consecutive days in the series against the Phillies. Four innings was a big ask. But he looked untouchable.

It was a tough question, albeit one with no bad answer.

"After his third inning, I looked at our pitching coach — let's see how he feels," Weiss said afterward. "If he feels good enough, I want to send him back out. I didn't want to mess with a good thing. He was throwing the ball really well."

So pitching coach Jeremy Hefner and coach Tony Diaz bounded over to Fuentes, resting nonchalantly on the dugout bench. In Spanish, Diaz asked how he felt — could he throw the ninth? Fuentes, unbothered, nodded and said yes. Diaz looked into his pitcher's eyes and tried to deduce the truth. Hefner did the same with Diaz. Satisfied with what they saw, the tandem returned to Weiss to relay the news: The ninth belonged to Fuentes.

"It's stuff you would never do in the regular season," Hefner told Yahoo Sports after Atlanta's series-tying 3-2 win .

Fuentes returned to the mound and retired the first two batters he faced before surrendering a last-gasp solo homer to Max Muncy. That brought Dodger Stadium alive. It also brought Weiss out of the dugout and Iglesias out of the pen. And the gambit worked. Pinch hitter Josue De Paula popped out harmlessly in foul territory to end the evening. Weiss and his crew patted one another on the back in congratulations. Fuentes, a wry smile peeking out from under his peach fuzz mustache, inched onto the field for celebratory handshakes.

With their ace Chris Sale in a hoodie, their best-laid bullpen plans shot to pieces and their heart rates through the roof, the Braves had stolen one from the Dodgers.

"It wasn't the plan, believe me," Weiss admitted postgame when asked about getting 11 outs from Fuentes.

Before the game, Weiss was grilled on his decision to push Sale to Game 3. The future Hall of Famer had been on schedule to throw Game 2 after starting Game 1 of the wild-card series on Tuesday . But an unlikely relief appearance on Thursday in Game 3 against Philadelphia changed things. Atlanta didn't want to squeeze dry its golden goose. A fully rested Sale, the Braves decided, offered the best odds of a series victory.

That meant employing a second straight bullpen game against the Dodgers in Game 2 on Sunday.

"Those are my favorite games," Hefner said afterward. "They are emotionally and intellectually exhausting. But it is the most fun to try to get the puzzle right."

Coincidentally, the Dodgers also found themselves in a bullpen game. Starter Blake Snell was discombobulated and ineffective in his first start of these playoffs. He walked five and needed 90 pitches to record 11 outs. While Snell avoided the big blow — Atlanta's only run against him came on a first-inning Mauricio Dubón infield single — it was a massively disappointing night for the two-time Cy Young Award winner.

"He just wasn't sharp, obviously," manager Dave Roberts said on the broadcast after taking out Snell. "He was fighting himself all game. You can see the fastball was good as far as life, velocity. But he didn't have command of that. The changeup, a pitch that he loves to go to, didn't have any feel for that. The slider, same thing.

"I think just tonight, he was just by himself. Obviously, the pitch count got up, and I just thought, that spot, we've gotta kinda limit the damage."

Snell's brief outing forced Roberts to boot up his own bullpen carousel. Combined, the teams used 11 relievers to cover 11 2/3 innings. It was a chaotic love letter to modern playoff baseball. At this time of year, there are no pitcher roles. There are just outs to collect, dreams to steal and legends to make.

For instance, Atlanta's scheduled "bulk guy," Grant Holmes, lasted just two-thirds of an inning. In the fourth, he allowed a game-tying solo shot from former Brave Freddie Freeman, Freeman's first extra-base hit since Sept. 2. Two more baserunners reached against Holmes, ending both his evening and the security of Atlanta's pitching plans. They went to setup man Dylan Lee in the fourth and former All-Star closer Robert Suarez in the fifth. The path to 27 outs looked fraught, with only Fuentes and Iglesias as trusted options.

But the Braves' offense retook the lead in the fifth as Los Angeles' bullpen game started to fray. Michael Harris II poked a two-out triple into the left-field corner, then scored on a Kris Bubic wild pitch. Harris, Atlanta's offensive star on the night, also provided some insurance in the seventh with a scorched RBI double that plated Matt Olson. That cushion proved crucial, as it allowed Weiss and Co. to keep leaning on Fuentes.

LA dodged major danger in the top of the eighth when Roki Sasaki, after loading the sacks with two walks (one intentional) and a hit-by-pitch, conjured an inning-ending double play from former MVP Ronald Acuña Jr. That threw the spotlight back onto Fuentes, the young swingman with the facial hair of a high school kid posing for a fake ID. But he was up to the moment, retiring Will Smith, Freeman and Teoscar Hernández in order in the eighth. Muncy made things hairy in the ninth, but Iglesias buckled down to tie this suddenly enticing series at one.

Sale, grounded in Game 2 against his wishes, will retake the stage on Tuesday. Opposite him, the Dodgers will tap Yoshinobu Yamamoto, last October's magic-maker. It's sure to be a firecracker, with two likely top-five Cy Young finalists squaring off with the series lead in the balance.

The coaches, at least, should have much less bullpen maneuvering to worry about.

articles.title: 6 Realistic MLB Trades That Could Happen In 2026-27 Offseason
articles.summary: While eight of Major League Baseball's 30 fanbases remain extremely invested in finding out who will win the 2026 World Series, nearly three-quarters of the league has already shifted into offseason mode.
articles.body:
While eight of Major League Baseball's 30 fanbases remain extremely invested in finding out who will win the 2026 World Series, nearly three-quarters of the league has already shifted into offseason mode.

And what a weird offseason it is going to be.

Whether we end up losing any or all of the 2027 season remains to be seen, but there's seemingly a 99.9 percent chance there will be a lockout when the current collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 without a new agreement in place—at which point teams can neither sign players to MLB contracts nor conduct any trades until the lockout ends.

That doesn't mean there won't be trades all offseason, though. Let's not forget the last time there was a lockout (2021-22), the A's traded away Matt Chapman, Matt Olson and Chris Bassitt within the first week back in business.

So, while the "when" part is quite up in the air, here are several swaps that could make sense for this offseason for all parties involved.

RHP Luis Gil (arbitration eligible through 2028)

LHP Ryan Weathers (arbitration eligible through 2028)

SS/3B/CF Caleb Bonemer (Double-A Prospect; No. 27 overall on MLB pipeline)

Max Fried is signed through 2032. Cam Schlittler won't hit free agency for the first time until after the 2031 campaign. And both Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón are signed through 2028.

The Yankees also have four more years of Will Warren, two years left on both Luis Gil and Ryan Weathers, one more season of Clarke Schmidt and two MLB-ready 23-year-olds in Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange.

That's quite the stockpile of starting pitching that they could use to perhaps pluck a quality prospect from a team that needs to bolster its rotation.

Speaking of positional surpluses, the Chicago White Sox have three players rated as top 100 prospects, per MLB.com's pipeline . All three are shortstops, including 2026 No. 1 overall draft pick, Roch Cholowsky.

But in Colson Montgomery and Chase Meidroth, the White Sox already have a middle infield tandem that is arguably top five in the majors in terms of defensive proficiency, plus Miguel Vargas fresh off an All-Star season at third base—and all three of those guys are under team control through at least 2029.

Recognizing this logjam (and his less-than-stellar glovework), they started giving Caleb Bonemer some reps in center field late in the 2026 season, giving him more paths to playing time in the majors after he clubbed 37 home runs in the minors this season.

Using him as a trade chip could also work, though, if the return is not one, but two starters who could be middle-of-the-rotation arms for them for the next two years.

Cleveland Guardians send : OF Steven Kwan (arbitration eligible in 2027)

Chicago Cubs send : RHP Jaxon Wiggins (Triple-A prospect) UTIL James Triantos (controllable through at least 2032)

Steven Kwan made $7.725M in arbitration for 2026. His 2027 salary is very likely to climb north of $10M.

And, well, unless it's for José Ramírez, the Guardians don't like dedicating eight figures to an individual player's salary.

At any rate, two winters ago, they traded away the final five seasons of their seven-year contract with Andrés Giménez, and subsequently shipped Josh Naylor to Arizona, rather than paying what ended up being a $10.9M salary in his final year of arbitration eligibility.

Despite their penny-pinching ways, they just keep making the postseason, winning the AL Central for the seventh time in 11 years.

So, if they can turn one year of Kwan into a pair of former second-round picks, history suggests they probably will.

On the Cubs' side of this one, they are losing a boatload this winter, including four of the six players who appeared in at least 20 games in the outfield in 2026. Pete Crow-Armstrong in center is a fantastic starting point, but Matt Shaw in right and either Justin Dean or Kevin Alcantara in left figures to be the plan as currently constructed.

"Losing a boatload" does also mean "has money to spend." But trading for one year of Kwan at $10M-$12M would allow them to do their real spending on the pitching staff, where they need it most.

Though Kwan is nowhere near the home run threat that Happ is, his career .739 OPS isn't drastically different from Happ's mark of .772 over the past five seasons. Both left fielders also won Gold Gloves in each of the past four years, so it could be quite the seamless transition.

On the prospects front, Jaxon Wiggins entered 2026 as a top 100 prospect on Baseball America, Baseball Prospectus and MLB, but he was a mess at Triple-A Iowa, walking nearly 20 percent of batters faced. Maybe Cleveland can fix his command, though, while James Triantos has .300 batting average / 30 stolen bases potential to replace Kwan.

Seattle Mariners send : RHP Logan Gilbert (arbitration eligible in 2027)

Minnesota Twins send : OF Emmanuel Rodriguez (controllable through at least 2032) RHP Riley Quick (Double-A prospect) IF Ben Ross (controllable through at least 2032)

First things first, the Mariners aren't throwing in the towel.

The 2026 season was a major disappointment, but they are still very much in their "win now" window. They just kind of have to hope/assume that Julio Rodríguez, Cal Raleigh and Josh Naylor bounce back from what was a combined OPS of roughly .680.

But between Emerson Hancock's breakout, Kade Anderson's arrival and Logan Gilbert's projected salary of $16M in his final year of arbitration eligibility, the M's might consider trading away the ace who was their Opening Day starter in both 2025 and 2026.

At any rate, this starting rotation would still be quite formidable even without Gilbert. In addition to Hancock and Anderson, Seattle has George Kirby (through 2028), Bryan Woo (through 2029) and Bryce Miller (through 2029) for another two years. Ryan Sloan is also one of the top pitching prospects in all of baseball, and he might be a factor by the end of 2027.

They aren't just going to salary dump Gilbert, though.

Seattle ought to be able to fetch a return on par with what the Brewers got for one year of Corbin Burnes and one year of Freddy Peralta in recent years—namely, an MLB-ready pitching prospect and a position player prospect who both rank around 100th overall.

So, who is arguably one quality pitcher away from becoming a contender in 2027 and has the means to put together that type of package?

But Minnesota might be most desperate of all, with Joe Ryan, Dean Kremer, Pablo López, Bailey Ober, Jeff Hoffman and Trevor Larnach each one year away from free agency and Byron Buxton not getting any younger.

The Twins wouldn't want to part with either Walker Jenkins or Kaelen Culpepper, but three guys a bit lower on their prospects list could be doable—with Emmanuel Rodriguez immediately becoming a candidate to fill the Randy Arozarena-sized hole in Seattle's outfield.

Aaron Boone Calls Out Yankees Catcher 🗣️

RHP Spencer Strider ($22M in 2027, $22M in 2028, $22M club option (or $5M buyout) for 2029

Outside of the rampant speculation of a possible Mason Miller blockbuster, the biggest non-trade of this year's deadline was the rumor that Spencer Strider might have gone to the Texas Rangers if Jacob deGrom hadn't invoked his no-trade clause to block it from happening.

When he was healthy, Strider was all sorts of special, arguably the best pitcher in all of baseball between the 2022 and 2023 campaigns. There were also flashes of his former dominance during the 2025 season, making 11 quality starts. But he missed almost all of 2024 and most of 2026 to injuries and might never get back to what he used to be.

Could the Braves revisit that attempt to get out from under the remainder of this contract?

And is anyone willing to help them do so?

Baltimore could be a great fit, especially if Atlanta is willing to retain some of the (at least) $49M still due to Strider.

At the moment, the Orioles' starting rotation for 2027 looks like Shane Baz, Kyle Bradish, Brandon Young and some serious question marks. And with Chris Bassitt, Zach Eflin, Andrew Kittredge and more coming off the books, they should have room in the budget to take a gamble on Strider.

At any rate, they're going to have to invest in pitching, unless they're irrationally confident in two of Cade Povich, Trey Gibson and Luis De León making an impact in 2027. Why not Strider if they can get him?

RHP Trevor Megill (arbitration eligible in 2027)

It's not officially the offseason until the Brewers trade away their final year of team control on a star player.

Traditionally, said player on the move is a pitcher.

Last winter, they sent Freddy Peralta to the Mets for a pair of prospects. The previous year, it was Devin Williams to the Yankees for Nestor Cortes and Caleb Durbin. The year before that, they traded Corbin Burnes to the Orioles for DL Hall and Joey Ortiz. And while they didn't do anything too big during the 2022-23 offseason, that's because they had already sent the Padres 1.5 years' worth of Josh Hader for four players at the 2022 trade deadline.

So, while they also have William Contreras prominently on their list of players who will hit free agency next winter, the Brewers trading away their final season of closer Trevor Megill might as well be the free space on the Bingo board of offseason trade predictions.

The 'where' part of the deal is much less of a freebie.

But do you know who really needs to address the back of its bullpen and is really sick and tired of facing Megill?

That would be the Pittsburgh Pirates, against whom Megill has made 18 appearances with a 0.51 ERA and 0.62 WHIP.

Pittsburgh finally had a winning season in 2026, but fell a few games shy of the much bigger goal of making it back to the postseason. Maybe Megill is the missing piece that gets them there.

And if Megill does get dealt, get ready for Abner Uribe to become the next All-Star closer in Milwaukee. They've got him under team control through 2030, and he has a 2.20 ERA through his first 182 big league appearances.

Colorado Rockies send : C Hunter Goodman (arbitration eligible through 2029)

Texas Rangers send : RHP Caden Scarborough (High-A prospect) RHP AJ Russell (High-A prospect) C Malcolm Moore (Double-A prospect)

Lost amid the embarrassment of the Rockies enduring yet another season of more than 100 losses, Hunter Goodman did quite a bit of mashing with 41 home runs in his 574 trips to the plate. That translates to a home run in 7.1 percent of his plate appearances, which was the highest ratio in the majors this season.

Before you even think about trying to chalk that up to Coors Field being Coors Field, note that for the second consecutive year, Goodman hit roughly 60 percent of his home runs on the road.

His power plays everywhere, and it's about time it gets to play for a contender.

Granted, Colorado's track record when it comes to trading away star players hasn't been great, to say the least. The Rockies didn't get much other than salary relief when they shipped out Ryan McMahon two summers ago. They never did manage to sell off Trevor Story before he hit free agency. And that Nolan Arenado trade back in February 2021 was an all-timer of a disaster.

But if they put him on the trade block and just wait for the offers to pour in, they should be able to get quite the haul for three years of Goodman's services.

For Texas, the catcher spot in the lineup was a season-long struggle and they have both Elias Díaz and Kyle Higashioka hitting free agency. They're also slated to lose primary DH Joc Pederson, so a slugging C/DH would be a huge pickup for them.

They're also pretty firmly in a "now or never" spot with their roster construction—Jacob deGrom turns 39 in June; Nathan Eovaldi turns 37 in February and has just one year left on his contract—and might be desperate enough to part with several of their top prospects.

articles.title: 7 MLB Players Worse Than You Think in 2026
articles.summary: For all the time spent this time of year on those who had special seasons, there is a flip side to that.
articles.body:
For all the time spent this time of year on those who had special seasons, there is a flip side to that.

Every year, there are a slew of players who underperform what was expected or projected of them coming into the season. Some are obvious, but others fly more under the radar.

Here's a look at seven MLB players who were worse than you think during the 2026 regular season.

Jose Altuve did homer in Game 2 of the ALWCS against the Chicago White Sox, his 28th career postseason homer. Only Manny Ramirez (29) has more in MLB history.

With that said, the former AL MVP isn't nearly the player he used to be. In his age-36 season, Altuve hit just .250, far below his .300 career batting average. And for the first time since the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, Altuve finished with an OPS+ below 100 (which is considered league average), posting a 97 in 2026.

What's more, he continues to be a nightmare in the field, as evidenced by his minus-17 defensive runs saved and minus-10 outs above average at second base this season. With Yordan Alvarez at DH and the experiment of Altuve in left field failing in 2025, there's not much they can do with their franchise icon defensively.

Altuve has a resume deserving of induction into the Hall of Fame, but the final three seasons of a five-year, $125 million deal could be ugly.

Brandon Marsh was one of the best stories of the first half of the 2026 season, getting voted to start in the All-Star Game for the National League at his home park after batting .301.

Following the All-Star break, though, he was one of the worst players in baseball by just about any metric. In the second half, he batted just .184 with a meager .502 OPS. By the end of the season, his 0.3 WAR was the eighth-worst mark among all qualified position players, per FanGraphs .

The Phillies could well bring Marsh back and hope for a resurgence during his contract year. However, having Otto Kemp pinch hit for him—even if it was against Chris Sale—with the season on the line felt pretty damning.

It would hardly be shocking if the Phillies, in need of a shake-up, consider trading Marsh this offseason .

Despite not being in contention, the Royals weren't really interested in moving Seth Lugo prior to the trade deadline, with USA Today's Bob Nightengale saying at the time that the team believes he'll be a key cog in a 2027 turnaround.

The problem with that is that Lugo posted a 6.12 ERA in 13 starts after the All-Star Break. Even prior to the Midsummer Classic, Lugo had a disappointing 4.56 ERA over 104.2 innings. He did log 172.1 innings pitched, but also led AL starters in both hits (200) and earned runs (99).

Lugo is just a couple seasons away from finishing runner-up in AL Cy Young voting, but he'll also pitch next season at 37 years old. Lugo is owed $21.5 million in 2027, with a conditional $17 million club option for 2028. Given the budget constraints president of baseball operations J.J. Picollo has to operate under, he may live to regret not moving Lugo when he had the chance.

Aaron Boone Calls Out Yankees Catcher 🗣️

Jo Adell is such a frustrating player, because his high-end flashes—be it homering 37 times in 2025 or robbing three homers in an April game—are so enticing. But 2026 is just another season where he didn't put it all together.

Adell felt like someone who would benefit greatly from a change of scenery, and finally got one in August when the Los Angeles Angels traded him to the Guardians. His production in 2026 was better in Cleveland than Anaheim, but he still only posted a .740 OPS in 48 games with the Guards.

To be fair to Adell, he has a place in the league as is. He mashed lefties this season, batting .320 with a .971 OPS against southpaws. Perhaps he should just be a platoon guy.

It's always felt like he had a higher ceiling than that, though. For him to finish the season with just a 0.6 WAR and 98 OPS+ is underwhelming. Perhaps a full year in Cleveland next year will lead to better results.

After trading him to the Texas Rangers at the 2025 deadline, the Diamondbacks brought back Merrill Kelly on a two-year, $40 million contract with a vesting option for a third season last winter.

Early returns suggest they may have gotten too sentimental in giving a guy heading into his age-37 season a multi-year deal.

Granted, he did log 162 innings this season, despite beginning the campaign on the injured list with left intercostal nerve irritation. But the Snakes didn't bring Kelly back to just be an innings eater, so they have to be concerned by the fact that the veteran righty posted a 4.94 ERA and 5.32 FIP.

It's difficult to know what to make of Arizona's rotation heading into 2027. Kelly will be 38, and coming off a disappointing year. Corbin Burnes made just three starts in his return from Tommy John surgery before having to go on the IL with shoulder inflammation.

In a season split between the San Francisco Giants and Padres, Robbie Ray did post a 3.59 ERA across 165.2 innings, which sounds pretty good if you don't dig any deeper into it.

However, his 3.08 ERA in 22 outings with the Giants seemed unsustainable considering it came with a 4.36 FIP. Indeed, he experienced a regression in nine starts after his trade to San Diego, with a 5.02 ERA in nine starts for the Friars. He then lasted just 2.2 innings in Game 1 of the NLDS against the Milwaukee Brewers, allowing four hits and two earned runs.

Ray does still carry value as a back-end starter who will eat innings, but the 35-year-old is past the stage of his career where he should be viewed as a frontline starter.

Even though he only hit seven home runs, Taylor Ward was pretty effective in 111 games for the Baltimore Orioles, doubling 20 times and drawing 87 walks.

Not only did a trade to Seattle, unsurprisingly, not reignite his power stroke, but Ward just completely hit a wall after being dealt to the Mariners. In 101 plate appearances with the M's, Ward hit just .125 with zero homers. After posting a .383 on-base percentage with the O's, Ward finished his brief Mariners stint with just a .238 OBP.

Obviously, Ward won't be back in Seattle. He'll be a difficult free agent to figure out. He homered 36 times and drove in 103 runs for the Angels in 2025. In 2026, he hit seven homers and drove in 37 runs in 143 games. He did walk 99 times, but it's hard to know what to expect from him moving forward.

articles.title: Inside Jackson Chourio’s late-game heroics that lifted Milwaukee Brewers over San Diego Padres in NLDS Game 2
articles.summary: In a thrilling finish, Jackson Chourio's walk-off single led the Milwaukee Brewers to a dramatic 4-3 victory over the San Diego Padres, giving them a 2-0 lead in the NLDS.
articles.body: Jackson Chourio delivered the signature moment for the Milwaukee Brewers in a dramatic 4-3 victory over the San Diego Padres in Game 2 of the National League Division Series. His two-out, two-strike single in the ninth inning sealed Milwaukee’s comeback and gave the Brewers a 2-0 lead in the series.The win came with Milwaukee trailing 3-2 in the bottom of the ninth, setting up Chourio’s big at-bat to be the game’s defining moment. Jackson Chourio hit a walk-off single in the ninth inning, and the Milwaukee Brewers beat the San Diego Padres 4-3.What Jackson Chourio did late to lift the Milwaukee Brewers over San Diego Padres in NLDS Game 2 Mason Miller was back out for another inning of work as Milwaukee entered the bottom of the ninth trailing 3-2. Christian Yelich started the rally with a walk and then stole second, and Sal Frelick walked, too.Andrew Vaughn struck out for an out, and Gary Sánchez walked to load the bases. That put Chourio in the batter's box with the game on the line.After a handful of triple-digit offerings, Miller challenged him with another high-velocity fastball. Chourio stayed ready, sat on a tough slider and finally lined a 101.3 mph fastball by second baseman Jake Cronenworth.Christian Yelich and Sal Frelick scored on the play, sending American Family Field into a frenzy.The victory gave the Brewers a 2-0 lead in the best-of-five NLDS. It was also Milwaukee’s first last-inning comeback in the postseason when trailing going into the final inning.The moment capped an impressive early postseason for Chourio. The young outfielder already had established himself as a major power threat, and now he added another big October performance against one of baseball’s most difficult closers.The Milwaukee Brewers now take momentum into Game 3 with a chance to finish the series on the road. Meanwhile, the San Diego Padres are fighting an uphill battle after blowing late leads in back-to-back games.Chourio’s performance reinforced a theme that has followed Milwaukee all season long: The Brewers are still capable of creating opportunities until the final out. With a single in the ninth inning, he turned what seemed like a frustrating loss into one of the franchise’s most dramatic postseason wins.Why the ninth inning mattered for both MLB teamsMilwaukee scored in the bottom of the ninth to stop the San Diego Padres from tying the series. Mason Miller already got the Brewers in the eighth and came back out to keep the lead.But Milwaukee's hitters didn't give away the last outs. Yelich, Frelick and Sanchez worked the inning more before Chourio had his second big chance of the night.That sequence made the victory all the more significant. The Brewers didn’t have one big early offensive explosion; they came back with disciplined plate appearances before Chourio put the exclamation point on it. Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young-winning lefty figures to be the most coveted piece. What is the latest on him and a pair of Cubs likely to find new teams?

Find out in this collection of rumors from the game's most trusted insiders and predictions for each player's landing spot.

"Most insiders project the Dodgers and Mets to be serious bidders, but there is some hesitation surrounding the Dodgers given the controversy around the team's ownership. Some thought the Mets might be looking to do a shorter-term deal such as they did with Bo Bichette, which might not work if Skubal is looking to set a record for guaranteed money."

Record money is likely in play for Skubal, too, given his production on the mound.

The two-time All-Star and Cy Young winner led the Majors in ERA the last two seasons and in 2025, recorded 7.30 strikeouts per walk, best in the sport. His 2026 was not as dynamic from a stat perspective, but it did see him join Los Angeles at the deadline and give that dynastic squad an opportunity to make a run at a third, consecutive World Series win.

It makes sense that the Dodgers would be in contention to retain his services, and the Mets are big spenders lacking an ace on the mound to pair with young thrower Nolan McLean.

Their ability to put together big-money deals, on the heels of others to Shohei Ohtani and Juan Soto, respectively, could be the difference between those two teams signing him, and an outside competitor, such as the Yankees or Braves, popping in and acquiring his services.

Prediction: Skubal ultimate re-signs with the Dodgers , especially if they win a championship this year

Following the Cubs' brief appearance and rapid departure from the 2026 playoffs, Patrick Mooney and Shahadev Sharma of The Athletic reported, "Considering their pitching deficit, it's unlikely that the Cubs will get into a bidding war for (Seiya) Suzuki's services, let alone win one."

Suzuki has long been one of the more reliable hitters for Chicago, with a career 16.2 WAR, 113 home runs and a .269 batting average, all with the Cubs.

This past season, he delivered 26 homers and 86 RBI.

Unfortunately for Chicago, they have bats, including the likely NL MVP, Pete Crow-Armstrong and prized free agent addition, Alex Bregman.

They need pitching, especially with Cade Horton, Justin Steele, Ben Brown, and Edward Cabrera all missing significant time this past season. The team needs to bolster their starting rotation and probably could use an arm or two in the bullpen, too.

The amount of money needed to make that happen makes a reunion with Suzuki nearly impossible, yet understandable.

Toronto, Philadelphia, the New York Yankees, and Los Angeles Dodgers are all teams with money to spend who could use an upgrade both at the plate and in the outfield.

The Blue Jays have already been linked to Suzuki by Mitch Bannon of The Athletic and with their desire to get back to World Series contention after a last-place finish this season, Suzuki is one way to kick things off with a bang.

Prediction: Suzuki leaves Chicago for Toronto and continues his consistent play for another contender

Ian Happ has been with the Cubs for the last decade but his time in the Windy City may be coming to an end, particularly after he saw his playing time decreased amid the arrival of Tyrone Taylor in a trade with the Mets.

As much as it may seem as though Happ is on his way out, and the veteran player has even discussed as much, a new report suggests that is not necessarily the case.

Mooney and Sharma reported, "As polarizing as Happ is among the fanbase, bringing him back on a team-friendly deal isn't entirely out of the question. He's an above-average performer at the plate, a four-time Gold Glove winner and a valuable presence in the clubhouse."

A player who saw his stats diminished exponentially in 2026 (.218/.326/.412), it will be interesting to see which teams take a shot on him assuming they are getting the Happ of two seasons ago, with the defensive skill set they are missing in the outfield.

articles.title: Dodgers 'Have to Go Through Heaven and Hell' as 'Nothing is Easy,' Says Rojas After Loss to Braves
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Dodgers have the second-highest payroll in baseball and a star-studded roster that has led them to the past two World Series titles. But that doesn't mean that earning the three-peat will be easy.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have the second-highest payroll in baseball and a star-studded roster that has led them to the past two World Series titles. But that doesn't mean that earning the three-peat will be easy.

"People think because we have a really good team, it should be easy. In baseball, nothing is easy," infielder Miguel Rojas told reporters on Sunday after the Dodgers lost Game 2 of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves, 3-2. "If we're going to do this, we're going to have to go through heaven and hell."

In Game 2, the Braves survived yet another bullpen game, with unlikely heroes in Ray Kerr and Didier Fuentes largely silencing the vaunted L.A. lineup. Shohei Ohtani remains mired in a slump, going his last 20 games without a homer. And the Dodgers will have to face ace Chris Sale in Game 3 back in Atlanta.

MLB playoff game among hottest ever in history

"I've been saying this for a long time now: I don't think people truly appreciate how hard it is to make a deep postseason run year in and year out," Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy noted. "You see it every year with teams that make these runs and the next year they're not even close to the same. They're hurt. They're worn out. They've got things going on. We've been able to weather that for a lot of years now. The Division Series is obviously not as much of a sprint as the Wild Card. But it's a sprint. It's five games. It's short. They're really, really tough to play."

articles.title: Willson Contreras Met With Red Sox Manager, Exec for 2 Hours After Comments Following Yankees Loss
articles.summary: Willson Contreras didn't mince words after the Boston Red Sox were swept by the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Round, seemingly taking aim at analytics in particular after Sonny Gray was pulled in the fifth inning of Game 2 despite throwing just 70 pitches and giving up just two earned runs.
articles.body:
Willson Contreras didn't mince words after the Boston Red Sox were swept by the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Round, seemingly taking aim at analytics in particular after Sonny Gray was pulled in the fifth inning of Game 2 despite throwing just 70 pitches and giving up just two earned runs.

"It's not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that's telling you what to do. Because this is baseball," Contreras told reporters. "And the data is here to help us. But at the end of the day, you're gonna have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."

Players Who Were Worse Than You Think in 2026 ⚾

On Monday, Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said he met with Contreras and manager Chad Tracy and had a constructive discussion.

"We met for over two hours and we talked about a host of things," he told reporters . "Many of those I will keep private just to kind of preserve the relationship that we have. But it was incredibly constructive and covered a wide scope of things. Willson would be the right person to ask directly, but he spoke very, very highly of his time here, how much he's looking forward to 2027 and the way that he and his family appreciated the Red Sox."

Contreras was not alone in his frustrations regarding the Gray decision, especially considering the bullpen went on to give up another seven runs.

"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that's a fact," Gray told reporters . "I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment."

Tracy, meanwhile, said the decision to pull Gray was his and wasn't a predetermined move coming from the front office or analytics department.

"The decisions are mine," he told reporters. "We have information, just like all the other 29 teams have information. Everybody has that. I've said this before: Since I've been here, do I sit in the office and talk through who's available throughout the entire season, who's available today, what's the best way to deploy them, who's down every single day? You do that. But not one time since I've been here has anybody scripted a game, has anybody told me, use this number right here to decide in this inning. Those decisions, they're mine. So as far as that specific one, my decision that obviously didn't go great. That falls on me. Do we have data, analytics? Of course we do. Everybody does. Is somebody standing there pushing me, saying, 'You need to do this, this, and this?' Absolutely not."

The Gray conversation—and pitching struggles overall during Wild Card Round—has somewhat overshadowed the fact that Boston's offense managed just two runs in the two losses against the Yankees.

Manny Ramírez was one of MLB's best hitters during his playing career. Now, he's hoping to parlay that accumulated knowledge into a coaching role.

The Chicago White Sox erupted for three runs in the sixth to stun the Cleveland Guardians, 4-3, and take a 2-0 lead in the American League Division Series on Monday.

The No. 2-seeded Guardians entered the matchup as 1.5-point favorites over the No. 6 White Sox, per FanDuel Sportsbook , but fell at home once again with a decisive Game 3 coming up on the road.

With the bases loaded in the bottom of the first, Guardians' Steven Kwan and Jose Ramirez scored on a throwing error by Sean Newcomb, who threw the ball past first base. Nathaniel Lowe notched an RBI, bringing home Kwan.

Cleveland's ace Williams got off to a hot start, striking out six through three innings and holding the White Sox scoreless throughout.

Things imploded for Williams in the sixth inning as he exited after giving up three runs and leaving a runner at second, with Chicago finding its offensive rhythm. Despite the rough inning, Williams finished with 11 strikeouts, tying the Guardians' second-most strikeouts in a postseason game.

Chicago's Munetaka Murakami brought home Kyle Teel in the top of the fourth for one run before a three-run sixth inning.

Braden Montgomery drove in two runs with a double, and Chase Meidroth brought Montgomery home to give the White Sox a 4-2 advantage after six innings.

In the bottom of the eighth, Jo Adell tripled to bring home Chase DeLauter and cut the deficit to one run heading into the final inning.

Closer Cade Smith then shut down the White Sox with a quick three outs, sending Cleveland to the bottom of the ninth needing at least one run to keep Game 2 alive.

White Sox closer Grant Taylor never broke a sweat, retiring the Guardians in order in the ninth to seal Game 2 with a chance to clinch it at home.

The two teams will make the switch to Chicago for Game 3 of the ALDS after Cleveland hosted the first two games. First pitch is scheduled for 4:00 p.m. ET on Wednesday.

articles.title: White Sox rally past Guardians bullpen, spoil 11-strikeout effort from Gavin Williams for 2-0 ALDS lead
articles.summary: Chicago is 4-0 in the postseason and one win away from advancing to the ALCS.
articles.body: Through five innings Monday, Cleveland Guardians ace Gavin Williams was pitching a playoff game to remember.Then the Chicago White Sox rallied against Cleveland's bullpen to spoil Williams' 11-strikeout effort and steal a 4-3 victory in Game 2 of the ALDS.With the win, the White Sox swept the first two games of the series on the road. They'll head to Chicago with a 2-0 series lead and two chances to close out the best-of-five series at home, with a spot in the ALCS at stake.White Sox bullpen game gets the win againThe White Sox countered Williams with another bullpen game that got off to a rough start when Cleveland's first two baserunners scored. But from there, Chicago's bullpen largely stymied Cleveland, led by 5 1/3 innings of one-hit ball from Sean Burke, who carried Chicago from the third inning into the eighth.Burke left the mound after issuing a two-out single to Chase DeLauter in the eighth. DeLauter then scored on a triple by Jo Adell off Grant Taylor that just missed clearing the high center-field wall.Then Taylor settled in to secure the final out of the frame and complete a four-out save in the ninth.Sox spoil Williams' big dayAt the plate, rookie slugger Munetaka Murakami delivered again, this time with an RBI single in the fourth off Williams to get the White Sox on the board and cut Cleveland's lead to 2-1.Munetaka Murakami drives in the White Sox first run! #Postseason pic.twitter.com/oBhQNV3Hpk— MLB (@MLB) October 5, 2026Williams didn't wilt with two men on and no outs. He closed out the frame with three straight outs, including a pair of strikeouts. He then recorded three more K's in the fifth to raise his strikeout tally to 11, one short of tying Cleveland's franchise record for a postseason game (Charles Nagy had 12 in 1996).But Williams issued a leadoff single to Miguel Vargas in the sixth. And at 98 pitches, his day was done. Manager Stephen Vogt pulled him in favor of reliever Erik Sabrowski, a move that immediately backfired.After getting one out, Sabrowski issued a walk to pinch hitter Randal Grichuk. Williams' brilliant starting effort on the mound was spoiled, and the White Sox turned a 2-1 deficit into a 3-2 lead.Before the sixth inning was over, Chase Meidroth added an insurance run on a single that scored Montgomery from second. On the heels of three consecutive 100-plus-loss seasons, the White Sox are 4-0 in their first postseason appearance since 2021. With one more win, they'll advance to their first ALCS since 2005, the year they won the World Series.Williams, meanwhile, is saddled with disappointment alongside his Guardians teammates after starting the day on pace to make history on the mound.

articles.title: Is the Dodgers dynasty already in jeopardy after brutal game two NLDS loss to Atlanta Braves?
articles.summary: Ray Kerr's shutout innings against the Dodgers in NLDS Game 2 show why even a Major League Baseball superteam can't guarantee a World Series repeat.
articles.body: "They're ruining baseball." "They've built a superteam." "They're unbeatable." "Too many fans and teams have no hope of their team reaching or winning the World Series." "Lock 'em out." MLB'S SALARY CAP PROPOSAL WON'T FIX THE LEAGUE'S NON-EXISTENT COMPETITIVE BALANCE PROBLEMS With some varying degree of consistency, all of these statements have become oft-repeated campaign phrases from either Major League Baseball itself or many of the league's fans. Mostly as a result of the Los Angeles Dodgers winning back-to-back World Series titles and continuing to add expensive players to their roster, despite the success. For much of the 2026 season, off-field discussion and PR efforts centered on the league's owners demanding a salary cap in upcoming labor negotiations, as a direct result of the Dodgers' spending. Curiously, few of these proponents ever mention the New York Mets and their spending. Interestingly, the Mets missing the postseason for two consecutive seasons despite a top-2 payroll never seems to come up. Nor the Giants and Angels futility, despite their big markets and payrolls. But beyond the labor discussion is the on-field results. Yes, the Dodgers have won the World Series in two straight years. And yes, there's still every opportunity for them to win a third title in 2026. The issue? Sunday night's game two of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves showed why there's no such thing as a foregone conclusion in baseball. Why it's not possible to "ruin" the most unpredictable sport in the country. And why assembling even the best roster guarantees nothing. The Dodgers won game one in mostly ho-hum fashion, with Tarik Skubal going six strong innings and Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernandez, and Max Muncy hitting home runs to win 5-3. When the Braves announced that superstar starter Chris Sale would be held back for game three, the widespread expectation was that the Dodgers had a tremendous advantage for game two. Blake Snell, a two-time NL Cy Young Award winner, was set up to start for LA. Atlanta? They countered with little-used reliever Ray Kerr. Kerr didn't pitch in the majors in 2025, had a 5.64 ERA in 2024, and has such poor "stuff" that he struck out just 11 hitters in 18.1 innings in the regular season. Game over, right? Of course not. The Dodgers missed every opportunity against the Atlanta bullpen, made several uncharacteristic mistakes, and lost game two 3-2 to even the series at one apiece. Kerr went 3.1 scoreless innings against the Philadelphia Phillies in a decisive game three of the wild card series. He followed that up by going 2.2 scoreless innings against the Dodgers in a pivotal Game 2 of the NLDS. Because of course he did. Outsider observers might point to Kerr's 1.47 ERA in his regular season sample as evidence that his postseason performance is justified. Except the underlying stats show how fortunate he was to have those results. Kerr's BABIP allowed, or batting average on balls in play, was .143 in the regular season. The league average is around .300. In 2024, his BABIP allowed was .403, demonstrating that there's no secret formula Kerr is using to over-perform. And it's not just BABIP. The league's average left on base percentage is around 75%, essentially, when baserunners reach against a pitcher, league average is that 75% of those runners won't score. Kerr's LOB% this year? 98%. Put simply, that's absurdly "lucky" and will regress to the mean over a broader sample. But that highlights the problem with trying to "predict" postseason baseball: over a small sample size, like a single series, or even a few series, a pitcher like Ray Kerr can throw six shutout innings against two of the best lineups in baseball. Sure enough, thus far in October, Kerr's BABIP allowed is .200 and his LOB% is 100%. Over an entire season, those numbers will not continue. It's impossible. But in a playoff series? In any series? It's not impossible or even improbable. The gaps between players in baseball are so small that on any given day, Ray Kerr can outpitch Blake Snell, who was mostly ineffective, over a few inning sample. Or Didier Fuentes, a good but inexperienced relief pitcher, can go 3.2 innings and allow just one run while retiring nine straight Dodger hitters. Suddenly, the unbeatable Dodgers dynasty is in serious trouble. It's one game, though, you might be thinking. And of course that's right; LA is still favored, slightly, to win the series. But Atlanta can now start Chris Sale on regular rest in game three, at home, not long after he threw a complete-game shutout against the Dodgers at Truist Park with 11 strikeouts and just five baserunners allowed. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE It's a new game, it's the playoffs, each start is independent of the last, but even with Yoshinobu Yamamoto starting for Los Angeles, the Braves likely have the advantage to win game three. Suddenly, what looked like a foregone conclusion could turn into a 2-1 Braves series lead by Tuesday night. And therein lies the problem. If your offense has an off night in a best-of-5, your season can end in a hurry. If your left fielder misplays a routine pop-up, like Teoscar Hernandez did on Sunday, your season can end in a hurry. If your relief pitcher throws a wild pitch after your defense allowed a gift triple, your season can end in a hurry. In LA's case, it's not just Sale, it's that their best hitter, Shohei Ohtani, clearly isn't healthy. Ohtani, though he has two singles in the NLDS, has not looked anything like the dominant force he often was in the 2025 playoffs. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! In his first at bat, Ohtani struck out on four pitches from Kerr, only one of which was even remotely close to the strike zone.
