articles.title: White Sox surge past Guardians 4-3 to take 2-0 lead in ALDS and move within 1 win of ALCS
articles.summary: Braden Montgomery lined a two-run double down the right-field line, Sean Burke allowed one hit in 5 1/3 innings of splendid relief and the Chicago White Sox beat the Cleveland Guardians 4-3 on Monday to take a 2-0 lead in their AL Division Series.
articles.body: Braden Montgomery lined a two-run double down the right-field line, Sean Burke allowed one hit in 5 1/3 innings of splendid relief and the Chicago White Sox beat the Cleveland Guardians 4-3 on Monday to take a 2-0 lead in their AL Division Series. The surprising White Sox improved to 4-0 in these playoffs — all on the road — and are one win from advancing to the American League Championship Series for the first time since winning the World Series in 2005. Chicago became the first team to reach the postseason after three straight 100-loss seasons, including a post-1900 record 121 defeats in 2024. Jo Adell hit an RBI triple in the eighth and Chase DeLauter had two hits for the Guardians. Starting pitcher Gavin Williams struck out 11, tied for second-most in a Cleveland postseason game. But the offense failed to produce for the second straight game. Grant Taylor worked 1 1/3 innings and allowed one hit as he got his second straight save. The best-of-five series shifts to Chicago for Game 3 on Wednesday. 3-run sixth propels the White Sox Kyle Teel got Chicago’s first hit with a single up the middle leading off the fourth. He advanced to second on Miguel Vargas’ walk and scored on Munetaka Murakami’s base hit to pull Chicago within 2-1. The White Sox went ahead with a three-run sixth. Vargas led off with a base hit to chase Williams and advanced to second on a groundout. Randal Grichuk drew a walk before Erik Sabrowski’s wild pitch with Tommy Pham at the plate advanced the runners to second and third. Pham flied out to shallow left before Montgomery jumped on a first-pitch fastball to drive in the go-ahead runs. Montgomery celebrated at first base before scoring on Chase Meidroth’s single to right. Williams allowed two runs and four hits in five-plus innings. Burke almost silences Cleveland’s bats Burke came on with one out in the third. After Travis Bazzana walked with one out in the fourth, the right-hander retired 13 straight until DeLauter had a base hit to left to end Burke’s night. Burke struck out six and threw 83 pitches, including 53 strikes. Taylor entered and allowed an RBI triple to Adell before Nathaniel Lowe flied out to end the inning. Guardians get on the board quickly After getting shut out on Saturday, the Guardians struck quickly with a pair of runs in the first inning. Steven Kwan led off with a base hit and José Ramírez drew a walk before Chase DeLauter’s grounder off opener Anthony Kay moved the runners to second and third. Sean Newcomb came on and intentionally walked Adell to load the bases. Lowe hit a high chopper to drive in Kwan, but Newcomb threw it wide of the bag at first, allowing Ramírez to score on the error. It marked the first time in four games this postseason the White Sox were behind. Kay faced three batters and threw 17 pitches, including eight strikes.

articles.title: Gavin Williams Meets The Moment, But Guardians Bats Let Him Down
articles.summary: Cleveland Guardians ace Gavin Williams put together one of the best outings of his big league career, but the Guardians didn't give him the run support he ne...
articles.body:
CLEVELAND - Everything lined up for the Cleveland Guardians the way they wanted after they won the AL Central. They earned the No. 2 seed and an automatic berth in the ALDS.

The Guardians seemed to draw the more favorable side of the bracket, avoiding the top-seeded Tampa Bay Rays - as well as their playoff nemesis New York Yankees - and they would be able to throw Parker Messick and Gavin Williams in Games 1, 2, 4 and 5.

The Guardians got a much-deserved week off last week to rest their weary legs after a grueling playoff push in September and they came into the postseason fresh and ready to compete.

Perhaps that's what makes the first two outcomes in Cleveland the last 72 hours all the more frustrating. After getting shut out in Game 1 on Saturday, 3-0, the Guardians coughed up an early 2-0 lead against the Chicago White Sox and dropped Game 2, 4-3 .

Gavin Williams followed Messick's solid outing in Game 1 with one of the best performances of his entire career, but Cleveland's offense hasn't done nearly enough to back their work. Now the Guardians are heading to Chicago to fight for their postseason lives.

Williams was completely overpowering on Monday night at Progressive Field.

He finished the game with 11 strikeouts, which is the second best performance in club postseason history. Only Charles Nagy in the 1996 ALDS against Baltimore has ever punched out more opposing hitters (12). Williams was the first Cleveland pitcher since Bartolo Colon in 2001 to strike out at least 11 hitters in a playoff game.

Williams' 55% miss rate was also the highest in his MLB career.

But it wasn't just that the White Sox had a hard time putting the ball in play. Williams "stuff" was as electric as he's ever showcased since making his big league debut on June 21, 2023.

Williams threw 36 of his 98 pitches at least 99.0 mph Monday night, and 18 of those registered triple-digits on the radar gun. It was one of the more memorable postseason pitching performances across the league since MLB began tracking advanced data.

Williams ultimately finished the night after 5-plus innings (he pitched to the leadoff hitter in the 6th). He surrendered two earned runs on four hits, scattering three walks and striking out 11.

He also made a little team history early in the game. With his strikeout of Murakami in the first inning, followed by fanning the side in the second, then opening the third inning with another K, Gavin Williams became the first player in Guardians franchise history to collect five straight strikeouts in a postseason game (according to Elias Sports).

Ultimately, the White Sox deserve a lot of credit for the way they made him work, especially the second time through the order. Chicago has been a bit strike-out-happy this year offensively anyways, and it didn't seem to overly fluster them that Williams had elite stuff on a big stage.

The bigger problem for Cleveland is that the offense has fallen flat through the first two games of the ALDS. The Guardians are 0-for-8 combined with runners in scoring position through the first two contests. Chicago gifted Cleveland a pair of runs on a throwing error in the first inning and it looked like perhaps "Guards Ball" could be the Sox undoing in Game 2.

But aside from Steven Kwan's first inning single and Chase DeLauter's second inning single, the Guardians didn't collect another base hit until the eighth inning.

In that regard, it felt a bit like Groundhog's Day for Guardians fans. The feeling is becoming a bit too familiar in watching October offensive struggles that don't back good pitching performances.

In fact, the Guardians are just 1-for-14 with runners on base in the first two games. That lone hit came off Jo Adell's bat in the 8th inning, after DeLauter had already singled. Adell tripled off the top of the fence in dead center field to bring home a third run.

Baseball Savant acknowledged the tracking data from Adell's long triple would have been a home run in 19 of 30 Major League ballparks.

It's probably unfair to over-react to losing back-to-back games with a subpar offensive output. It's happened plenty of times to this club all season and there doesn't seem to be any panic in the Guardians clubhouse after another loss.

And if history is any precursor, the Guardians are going to need to figure it out offensively because their postseason record with low run production isn't very good. Since 2017, Cleveland has lost 18 of 21 postseason games when scoring three-or-fewer runs. They've also won 9 of 11 when scoring at least four runs.

Stephen Vogt hasn't named his Game 3 starter yet, but whoever is on the bump is likely going to need a much better offensive output to stave off another long winter along the shores of Lake Erie.

Meanwhile, the White Sox haven't clinched a postseason series in front of a home crowd since they won the 1906 World Series over their northern neighbors from Wrigleyville.

Sox manager Will Venable acknowledged postgame that the White Sox altered their pitching plan when they saw the Guardians lineup for Game 2. Instead of going right from Anthony Kay to Sean Burke, he said they wanted to get through DeLauter a second time before going to Burke out of the bullpen. He decided to slot in Sean Newcomb, and went to him quickly after Kay pitched to just three hitters. Newcomb's throwing error allowed two Guardians runs to score in the first inning, but he ultimately got out of the inning without further damage. Burke was brilliant once he came in, at one point retiring 13 in a row and surrendering just one hit. He now has an ERA of less than 1.00 against Cleveland this season.

The Guardians recognize there is no room for error and if they want to snap the sport's longest World Series drought, Wednesday afternoon in the Windy City needs to see different results. 78 years was a long time ago.

articles.title: Yankees Errors Lead to Game 2 Loss to Rays, Box Score Stats, Highlights, Updated MLB Playoff Bracket
articles.summary: Four errors paved the way for the New York Yankees' Game 2, 5-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays on Monday, dropping them to 0-2 in the American League Divisional Series on the road.
articles.body:
Four errors paved the way for the New York Yankees' Game 2, 5-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays on Monday, dropping them to 0-2 in the American League Divisional Series on the road.

With their backs against the wall and down 0-1, the Yankees entered as 1.5-point favorites over the Rays, per FanDuel Sportsbook , with Cam Schlittler starting on the mound.

Schlittler finished the regular season tied for third in MLB with 239 strikeouts, entering the postseason as one of the Yankees' biggest weapons.

He backed it up in his first playoff start, a win over the Boston Red Sox, allowing just two hits while striking out 10. But Monday was a different story, as he surrendered seven hits, managed just two strikeouts and gave up two earned runs.

Tampa Bay struck first, with its first three batters reaching base in the first inning. Yandy Díaz scored on a throwing error by second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. after Junior Caminero grounded into a fielder's choice.

Schlittler and the Yankees escaped the bottom of the first with minimal damage, allowing one run despite a disastrous start that included three errors, stranding two runners at the corners.

The Yankees answered in the bottom of the third when Ben Rice launched a 372-foot solo home run to tie the game at 1-1.

It was a busy fifth inning for the Rays.

With two runners in scoring position, Liam Hicks grounded out to second to bring home Jonathan Aranda. Chandler Simpson followed with an RBI single after another Yankees miscue, giving Tampa Bay a 3-2 lead in the bottom of the fifth and prompting the Yankees to pull Schlittler.

Building on their lead, Richie Palacios ripped a line drive for a two-run double, bringing home Trent Grisham and Simpson to stretch Tampa Bay's lead to 5-1.

Rice capped a big night with his second home run in the top of the eighth, accounting for both of the Yankees' runs. But with one final chance in the ninth and trailing 5-2, New York went down in order to fall to 0-2 in the ALDS.

The two teams will head to New York for Game 3, where the Yankees will look to avoid a sweep at Yankee Stadium on Thursday. First pitch is scheduled for 8:00 p.m. ET.

articles.title: Yankees make 4 errors in sloppy loss to Rays, fall behind 2-0 in ALDS
articles.summary: The Yankees are one loss from falling short of a 28th World Series title for the 17th straight season.
articles.body: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Sloppy defense put the New York Yankees on the brink of elimination. Four errors and another defensive miscue led to three unearned runs that a lineup missing three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge couldn’t overcome in a 5-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of their AL Division Series on Monday night. The Yankees are one loss from falling short of a 28th World Series title for the 17th straight season. Even with likely AL Cy Young Award winner Cam Schlittler on the mound, the Yankees couldn’t even the best-of-five series against the pesky Rays. The small-ball Rays chased Schlittler in the fifth, aided by New York’s miscues in the field as the Yankees’ defense unraveled the same way it did in the team’s most recent World Series game two years ago against the Los Angeles Dodgers. Jonathan Aranda lined a single off Schlittler to start the bottom of the fifth and Junior Caminero ripped a double to right-center. With the infield drawn in except second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., who was standing several feet farther back on the dirt, Liam Hicks hit a slow bouncer to second that scored Aranda for a 2-1 lead. Chisholm’s only play was at first because he wasn’t all the way in like the rest of the infielders. Chandler Simpson then hit a grounder that rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. booted, scoring Caminero to make it 3-1. It was initially ruled a hit and then changed to an error and eventually a fielder’s choice. Brent Headrick replaced Schlittler and struck out Victor Mesa Jr. After Simpson stole second, Jonny DeLuca reached on a grounder when Lombard’s throw to first was wide for New York’s fourth error. Richie Palacios followed with a two-run single to center that increased Tampa Bay’s lead to 5-1. Ben Rice connected for his second homer of the game in the eighth but that wasn’t enough. The night started poorly for the Yankees. New York became the first team to commit three errors in the first inning of a postseason game since the Oakland Athletics in Game 1 of the 1975 American League Championship Series against Boston, according to Sportsnet Stats. Third baseman Ryan McMahon misplayed a bouncer by Yandy Díaz to begin the bottom of the first. After Aranda singled, Caminero hit a bouncer up the middle. Lombard fielded the ball behind the bag and flipped to second for a forceout, but Chisholm’s ill-advised, off-balance throw to first sailed wide, allowing Díaz to score and Caminero to reach second. Hicks then struck out but reached on catcher’s interference, with an error charged to Austin Wells. The 21-year-old Lombard then saved Chisholm from another error when he extended to catch a high toss to second following a sharp grounder by Simpson. Lombard came off the bag and quickly reached back with his leg to beat Hicks and get the second out. Schlittler retired Mesa on a grounder to prevent more damage. The Yankees infamously fell apart on defense in the fifth inning of Game 5 in the 2024 World Series. Leading 5-0 with Gerrit Cole on the mound, New York committed two errors and a mental lapse while allowing five unearned runs to score, and the Dodgers went on to win the game and clinch the championship.

articles.title: Rays chase Cam Schlittler, seize on 4 Yankees errors to take 2-0 ALDS lead
articles.summary: Tampa Bay is now 2-0 in the postseason and has reaffirmed its status as the team to beat in the American League.
articles.body: Facing a 1-0 ALDS deficit against the Tampa Bay Rays, the New York Yankees hoped presumptive Cy Young Award winner Cam Schlittler would be the salve to lead them to a Game 2 win.He was not.The Yankees started Game 2 on Monday in Tampa with a disastrous first inning on defense that featured three errors. That set the tone for a mistake-filled night and an eventual 5-2 Rays victory that gave Tampa Bay a 2-0 series lead.With the win, the Rays move to one win away from victory in the best-of-five series and a place in the ALCS. Defense fails Schlittler, YankeesTo be fair to Schlittler, the bulk of Monday's blame doesn't lie with him. That honor goes to a defense that committed four errors and could have been credited with five. The result of those errors was three unearned runs that proved to be the difference in Tampa Bay's win. And the three-error first inning forced Schlittler to throw 19 pitches on a night when he didn't make it out of the fifth.An offense that managed two runs against Freddy Peralta and Tampa Bay's bullpen didn't help.An errant throw by Jazz Chisholm Jr. was one of four Yankees errors on the night.Julio Aguilar via Getty ImagesIt added up to more disappointment for a Yankees team that left the wild-card round on a high after storming through a 2-0 sweep of the rival Boston Red Sox by a collective score of 18-2.But a Rays team that won the AL East with the best record in the American League is a different beast than the Red Sox. And through two games of the ALDS, Tampa Bay has reaffirmed its status as the team to beat in the AL.Yankees miscues start with first Tampa Bay at-batFor the Yankees, Tampa Bay's first at-bat proved ominous. Schlittler induced what looked like a routine ground ball from Yandy Díaz to third base. But the ball bounced off third baseman Ryan McMahon's glove for an error, allowing Díaz to reach safely.Ryan McMahon with an egregious error at third base to start Game 2 in Tampa Bay pic.twitter.com/MyLDIHalB2— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) October 6, 2026 Two batters later, with runners on first and second, second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. botched his part of a would-be double play with an errant throw to first base that bounced off the Tampa Bay dugout.That allowed Díaz to score the first of Tampa Bay's three unearned runs without a play at the plate. The Rays score first in ALDS Game 2! pic.twitter.com/H44QiuPjq3— MLB (@MLB) October 6, 2026 A third error on a catcher's interference call on Austin Wells didn't impact the scoring column. But it meant more work for Schlittler as he labored through the first inning. The Yankees were fortunate to leave the frame with only a 1-0 deficit. But the mistakes were a sign of things to come. Rays break it open, chase Schlittler in mistake-filled fifth inningAfter a Ben Rice solo home run in the fourth, the game was tied 1-1 heading into the fifth, and Schlittler had settled down the previous inning with his first 1-2-3 frame of the night. It proved to be his only one.Jonathan Aranda led off the bottom of the fifth with a rope to right field for a single, and Junior Caminero put runners on second and third with a double. Aranda then scored on a groundout for a 2-1 Rays lead. Then New York's defense failed Schlittler again. Rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. booted a ground ball that should have resulted in an out. Instead, it allowed Caminero to score and Chandler Simpson to reach first safely. George Lombard Jr. tries to hurry the throw and everyone is safe. 3-1 Rays pic.twitter.com/H8n2bsXGGv— Talkin' Yanks (@TalkinYanks) October 6, 2026 This was the could-be error that wasn't. Official scorers went back and forth on the play before settling on calling it a fielder's choice.Either way, it was the end of Schlittler's night. Manager Aaron Boone pulled his ace after 76 pitches with one out in the bottom of the fifth and the game threatening to get out of hand (which it did).An official Lombard error came two batters later. An errant throw to first with two outs allowed Jonny DeLuca to reach first safely and extend the inning.George Lombard Jr. is the fourth Yankee to make an error tonight pic.twitter.com/jW6tkbN0i9— Talkin' Yanks (@TalkinYanks) October 6, 2026 After DeLuca stole second, Richie Palacios capitalized in the next at-bat, with a rocket to center field that scored Simpson and DeLuca.Keep 'em runnin' Richie#ForTampaBay | #Postseason pic.twitter.com/vR1TJNjhgG— Tampa Bay Rays (@RaysBaseball) October 6, 2026 Those two unearned runs extended Tampa Bay's lead to 5-1 and ultimately put the game out of the Yankees' reach.Ben Rice’s heroics not enoughBen Rice did his best for the Yankees on Monday, as he did throughout a breakout regular season and playoffs. He hit his second home run of the night and his fourth of the postseason in the eighth inning to chip into Tampa Bay's lead.Ben Rice two-homer game!His second multi-HR game of the #Postseason pic.twitter.com/KKcCKDnHN2— MLB (@MLB) October 6, 2026 Both of his home runs Monday were solo shots. And they were all the Yankees managed against four Tampa Bay pitchers who combined to limit New York to four hits and two walks. Peralta pitched 4 2/3 innings, allowing 1 earned run on 3 hits and 1 walk with 3 strikeouts. All-Star closer Bryan Baker pitched a perfect ninth to ice the victory and earn his second save in two postseason games.Will Schlittler get another chance?As for Schlittler, he finished his night surrendering 4 runs — 2 of them earned — on 6 hits and 1 walk with 2 strikeouts in 4 1/3 innings. This could be his last appearance of the season, after which he's expected to be handed the AL Cy Young hardware. Alternatively, the Yankees would hand him the ball for a Game 5 on Saturday in Tampa. But they need to win Games 3 and 4 to get there. The good news for New York is the series shifts to the Bronx for those contests, starting with Game 3 at 8 p.m. ET Wednesday.

articles.title: Unlikely hero Braden Montgomery comes through for White Sox as they rally to take 2-0 ALDS lead vs. Guardians
articles.summary: "It's a feeling like no other," Montgomery said after Chicago's 4-3 victory. "You want to replicate that feeling every night."
articles.body:
CLEVELAND — When White Sox rookie right fielder Braden Montgomery strolled to the plate in the top of the sixth inning of ALDS Game 2 on Monday in Cleveland , the math was not on his side.

In the postseason, managers hunt matchups relentlessly. Lineup construction is delicate. Platoon advantages are pivotal. Deploying pinch-hitters and relievers at optimal junctures is paramount to success.

Skippers Stephen Vogt and Will Venable had spent the sixth inning seeking such edges. Cleveland right-handed starter Gavin Williams, having struck out 11 through five frames, returned to the mound with a 2-1 lead in the sixth. With lefty reliever Erik Sabrowski warming in the bullpen and dangerous left-handed slugger Munetaka Murakami looming on deck, Williams' final task was to retire Chicago's top righty bat, Miguel Vargas.

Instead Vargas singled, giving Chicago a leadoff baserunner and ending Williams' outing on an ominous note.

Sabrowski entered and kept Chicago's biggest bat quiet as planned, coaxing a groundout from Murakami that advanced Vargas to second. Then it was Venable's turn to counter by pinch-hitting his two veteran righty bats, Randal Grichuk and Tommy Pham. Grichuk walked. A wild pitch from Sabrowski advanced the runners to second and third. Pham flew out.

Then it was Montgomery's turn. On first glance, the 23-year-old's switch-hitting capability seemed like a boon in this situation, giving Chicago a third consecutive right-handed at-bat against Sabrowski, now with two runners in scoring position. But history indicated otherwise.

Montgomery's production from the right side has lagged behind his left-handed cut since his days as a celebrated amateur prospect. And once he arrived in the majors this season, that weakness was exposed to the extreme: Montgomery hit .129/.204/.226 across 103 right-handed plate appearances. His .430 OPS ranked 169th among 169 righty batters to record at least 100 plate appearances against left-handed pitching.

Making matters worse: Righty bats also struggled against the southpaw Sabrowski to an outlier degree. Only three left-handers (Josh Hader, Jacob Latz, Blake Snell) held right-handed bats to a lower OPS than Sabrowski (.510) in the regular season.

On paper, it would've been tough to draw up an at-bat that tilted more in the pitcher's favor. But this was not a computer simulation based on probabilities. This was October baseball in real life.

"Be ready to compete," Montgomery said afterward of his mindset. "That's the goal at the end of the day because numbers are what they are. It's the past, and so you use those experiences to sculpt what you believe to be the best way forward."

Montgomery pounced on a first-pitch fastball. The ball jumped off his bat at 101.4 mph and sizzled into right field, landing just inside the foul line, allowing Vargas and Grichuk to score easily and Montgomery to coast into second base.

"To see the ball get down and to know you've got two ducks on the pond … it's exhilarating," Montgomery said. "I was just running with the wind. It was special to touch the bag and look back into the dugout to see my guys."

With one swing, Montgomery flushed his statistical priors and flipped the script of ALDS Game 2 en route to a 4-3 Chicago victory . The math said the inning should've been over. The scoreboard said 3-2 White Sox.

To be fair, this was not Montgomery's first big moment of the year. Four months ago, he became the fifth player in MLB history to hit a walk-off home run in his major-league debut. That was an instant highlight for a rookie campaign that proceeded to be rather rocky; Montgomery posted a .651 OPS the rest of the way. But those struggles — and his becoming a passenger on Chicago's roller-coaster ride from deep rebuild to dominating in October — set the stage for a new kind of feeling on Monday.

"The first game up, I was welcomed in and enjoyed every moment of it," Montgomery said of his debut. "But I feel like it's impossible to feel like you're a part of the team at that point because I'm coming up two months into the season, I've been playing my own games six days a week. … I don't know what's been going on in the clubhouse or how they've been doing. So that felt more personal, that night.

"Tonight tops it tenfold," he continued, still beaming hours later. "To have those emotions going into it, to have been down the road with this team and be in these games and to be playing the most important baseball of the year. … It's a feeling like no other. You want to replicate that feeling every night."

That feeling — turning a Chicago deficit into a lead — was also something new for Montgomery and his teammates this postseason. The White Sox did not trail at any point during their two-game sweep of Houston in the wild-card series . In ALDS Game 1, five White Sox pitchers shut out the Guardians 3-0 . So when Cleveland jumped to a 2-0 lead in the first inning of Game 2 — on a bases-loaded throwing error, no less — it was the first time Chicago had been playing from behind since the third inning of Game 162.

But these White Sox, undaunted, methodically climbed back into the ballgame. They swung-and-missed a ton against Williams but also pushed his pitch count up early. They got on the board in the fourth inning via an RBI single from Murakami. In the home halves, Cleveland's bats remained quiet against Chicago's latest remix of relievers. Bulk pitcher Sean Burke breezed through five no-hit (!) innings after entering in the third. That complete lack of offensive momentum for the Guardians made way for Chicago's sixth-inning rally, and Chase Meidroth followed Montgomery's double with an RBI knock of his own, scoring what proved to be a vital insurance run.

Just once in Game 2 did a Cleveland batter produce a batted ball of real substance. After Burke allowed his first hit of the game with two outs in the eighth inning, Venable called on Grant Taylor — two days removed from his four-inning save in Game 1 — to face Jo Adell. Cleveland's DH, 0-for-6 with six strikeouts in the series before stepping in against Taylor, crushed a first-pitch fastball off the top of the left-field wall for an RBI triple that made it a one-run game. At a projected 413 feet, it was the farthest batted ball at Progressive Field this season that did not go for a home run.

"Stay in the ballpark, please," Taylor recalled thinking when Adell connected. "Thankfully, it stayed in — got a pretty tall wall over there."

Taylor's ninth inning was less eventful. He needed five pitches to retire the side in order, a fittingly flat finish to another uninspiring collective effort by the Guardians' offense — or, alternatively, a stress-free finale to another tremendous job by the White Sox pitching staff, with Taylor once again at the center of it.

One week ago, the White Sox were not guaranteed to host a home postseason game, having squandered a chance at the AL Central title and a first-round bye. But after four straight road victories to begin their improbable postseason run, Chicago will return to Rate Field needing just one win to advance to its first ALCS since the franchise's World Series run in 2005.

"I'm so excited," Montgomery said. "I can't place any expectations on it. I just know it's going to be special. I mean, seeing all the Sox fans here postgame and seeing the excitement they've had. … I can only imagine how the South Side is going to pop out in a couple of days.

"I can't wait to see it and be part of it."

articles.title: Ben Rice can't do it alone: Yankees face elimination after another offensive letdown
articles.summary: In the wake of the Yankees' 5-2 loss Monday night at Tropicana Field, the offense is another culprit also pushing them toward elimination.
articles.body:
The Yankees ' dreadful defense in Game 2 is certainly the headlining woe. It's the one that forced Cam Schlittler to throw stress-laden pitches in the first inning that doubtless impacted the rest of his outing. And it's the one that helped the Rays to three unearned runs.

But in the wake of the Yankees' 5-2 loss Monday night at Tropicana Field , there's another culprit also pushing them toward elimination:

It's every Yankee fan's October nightmare: the pinstriped bats have gone cold and there's no Aaron Judge coming to save them, at least in this series. He's out with a calf injury. After a splurge against the fading Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, the Bronx Bombers have turned that nickname into a punch line of sorts in this best-of-five AL Division Series against Tampa Bay.

"Whatever it takes, we've got to do it offensively and we've gotta be able to score some runs and do a better job of preventing (them,)" Aaron Boone said in the postgame news conference room.

It can only get better, right? In two games against the Rays, the Yankees have scored exactly twice. Both runs came in Game 2, when Ben Rice slammed two solo home runs. They have all of five hits -- Rice's home runs, two doubles by Austin Wells and a single by Cody Bellinger . They are 5-for-58 in the series (.086) with a .145 on-base percentage, .224 slugging and .369 OPS.

It's the fewest hits and fewest runs of any team in Division Series play. The Yankees, who drew the eighth-most walks in baseball during the regular season, aren't even doing that -- they have two walks in each game so far.

They have just four plate appearances with runners in scoring position in the series and are 0-for-2 with two walks.

Credit where it's due -- the Rays are pitching very well, from Drew Rasmussen in Game 1 to Freddy Peralta and the bullpen in Game 2.

And that is certainly part of the reason why, when they've had chances against Tampa Bay, the Yankees have missed. Wells foolishly tried to stretch an easy double into a triple in Game 1 and was easily thrown out, burying the only Yankee scoring chance against Rasmussen.

In Game 2, Bellinger, who batted .340 with runners in scoring position during the season and hit a big home run in the Boston series, came up with the bases loaded in the fifth inning and mashed a ball to center. It traveled 405 feet, but it was nothing more than a loud out, a ball with an expected batting average, per Statcast, of .760 that was caught on the warning track.

Boone noted that Bellinger's ball, a few feet either way, could've been a bases-clearing, series-changing double. And it was just one of six balls the Yankees hit 100-plus mph in Game 2, two fewer than the Rays.

"I thought we started to put together some really good at-bats, especially in the fifth inning where we chased Peralta and Belli puts a good swing on it, hits it to the fence," Boone said. "That's unfortunate there."

Rice, though, is doing real damage. He has driven in eight of the 20 runs the Yankees have scored in the postseason and he has four home runs, which leads all playoff hitters. He's the first Yankee to have more than one multi-homer game in the same postseason, according to Sarah Langs of MLB.com. He's batting .467 with an 1.889 OPS.

The Yanks will need some teammates to join him to get back in this series. It's already a daunting assignment: According to Langs, in all best-of-five postseason series, teams that go up, 2-0, win 89 percent of the time (83-of-93). In the current 2-2-1 home format, the team that wins the first two at home wins the series 92 percent of the time.

There's a lot to clean up. The defense better be good Wednesday night in Game 3 with groundball artist Max Fried starting for the Yankees.

And Rice can't be the only one raking, either. The Yankees haven't shown they can score enough against the Rays.

articles.title: Guardians’ ‘Sudden’ 6-time All-Star dies at 84
articles.summary: The 15-year MLB veteran also pitched for the Yankees, Giants and Pirates.
articles.body:
"Sudden" Sam McDowell, a 6-time All-Star pitcher for the Cleveland Indians who finished his career with the San Francisco Giants , New York Yankees and Pittsburgh Pirates has died. He was 84.

Bob Pompeani of KDKA in Pittsburgh reported that McDowell died Monday, Oct. 5.

In a 15-year career in MLB , McDowell struck out 2,453 batters — eighth on baseball's career list when he retired, and No. 46 all-time today. He led the American League in strikeouts five times.

McDowell retired with a 141-134 record and a 3.17 ERA.

A Pittsburgh native, McDowell debuted at 18 in September 1961. Four years later, he led the AL in ERA (2.18), struck out a career-high 325 batters, and made his first American League All-Star team.

However, his career was derailed by alcohol abuse, a vice he chronicled in depth in his 2025 memoir , "The Saga of Sudden Sam: The Rise, Fall, and Redemption of Sam McDowell." He pitched his final game for the Pirates as a 32-year-old in 1975.

After retiring as a player, McDowell counseled athletes who struggled with drug and alcohol abuse — not only in MLB but in the NFL and NHL as well .

"I remember when I got out of rehab, I must have called that man every day, at every hour of the night, for four straight months," former big league pitcher Mike York told the Los Angeles Times . "I mean, I was calling him at 5 in the morning, midnight, it didn't matter. He was always there when I needed him."

McDowell was the Baseball Assistance Team's addiction and recovery consultant from 1987-2016.

McDowell had two children, Debbie and Tim.

articles.title: Freddy Peralta proud of Rays bats for attacking Cam Schlittler
articles.summary: Freddy Peralta, the Tampa Bay Rays’ starter for Game 2 of the ALDS against the New York Yankees, lasted just 4.2 innings on the night, allowing one run on a...
articles.body:
Freddy Peralta , the Tampa Bay Rays ' starter for Game 2 of the ALDS against the New York Yankees, lasted just 4.2 innings on the night, allowing one run on a long ball from Ben Rice. But that scarcely mattered, even in a matchup against Cam Schlittler , the frontrunner for the 2026 AL Cy Young award.

Peralta got the run support he needed from the Rays hitters, with Tampa Bay scoring four of their five runs on the night in a 5-2 win over the Yankees in the fifth inning. The Yankees felt as though they had to pull Schlittler from the game after just 76 pitches after he had allowed two runs to cross the plate.

Putting runs on the board against Schlittler is no mean feat, and Peralta knows it. After the game, the Rays starter tipped his cap to his teammates, crediting them for being aggressive against the Yankees ace.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"I think that we are amazing in general, man. These guys, you can see the confidence when they are going to the plate, doing the little things in every at-bat. I think that the confidence, you can tell the confidence when they are stepping on the bus. I'm really proud of them, and you know, I enjoy with them. Together," Peralta told reporters after the game, via Ryan Bass of MLB TV.

The Rays do put pressure on the opposition by putting balls in play, and the Yankees defense floundered. New York committed four errors on the night, and Tampa Bay deserves the credit for putting them in a position to make those blunders.

Peralta also has to be feeling lucky about his fortunes this season. He went from underperforming for a disastrous New York Mets squad to pitching in the postseason for the Moneyball Rays . In 10 starts for the Rays in the regular season, he posted an ERA of 3.25 in 55.1 innings of work.

Now, the Rays need to win just one more game to dispatch of the Yankees and advance to the ALCS — with Nick Martinez leading the charge from the mound in Game 3 on Wednesday.

articles.title: Dodgers’ Freedie Freeman reveals exactly what Los Angeles needs to change
articles.summary: What do the Dodgers need to do?
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers haven't played the best baseball through the first two games of this NLDS against the Atlanta Braves , losing 3-2 on Sunday night after an impressive 5-3 win in Game 1.

For Los Angeles, it always seems like it'll find a way to win games. But this is baseball at the end of the day, and if it doesn't come out and take care of business, the Braves will take advantage. Atlanta is a veteran-led team from top to bottom with a boatload of talent.

The process hasn't been perfect for the Dodgers, either, as they've struggled to scrape together runs in multiple ways.

While home runs are typically how teams score in Major League Baseball nowadays, the Dodgers are relying on the long ball a bit too much, at least according to superstar Freddie Freeman.

"Gotta find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run; that's our biggest thing right now."

"Two really good teams going at it," Freeman added , per H/T Dodgers Blue.

Freeman left the yard in Sunday night's loss, blasting a solo shot in what was a two-hit night for the future Hall of Famer.

Otherwise, the Dodgers collected only six hits and couldn't get anything going against Didier Fuentes, who threw 3.2 innings of one-hit baseball, striking out three and walking zero.

The Dodgers are going to have to put together some very good at-bats in Game 3, as left-hander Chris Sale, one of the best we've ever seen, will toe the tilt.

articles.title: Phillies’ Bryce Harper named as trade candidate for Blue Jays, but it shouldn’t ever happen
articles.summary: They shouldn't even consider this.
articles.body:
The Philadelphia Phillies have undoubtedly been among the most disappointing teams in Major League Baseball over the past couple of seasons, and that has to change.

It's unfortunate that Philadelphia has played at this level recently, but it doesn't look like it's going to change in the near future. The Phillies find themselves in a very bad spot because of some of the contracts that they've handed out.

There's also a side of the story that suggests the Phillies will keep struggling because they likely won't want to move on from certain guys, and probably shouldn't.

That includes superstar Bryce Harper, who has been among the best players in Major League Baseball over the past decade-plus. As for what Philadelphia could do with Harper, there's actually no reason to move on from a guy like that.

If anything, the Phillies should be looking to move on from others to improve around Harper.

However, others don't believe that's the case, with one writer recently suggesting that the Toronto Blue Jays should be interested if he becomes available.

"How aggressive will the Blue Jays be after missing the postseason? Great question," Jake Elman wrote . "They're possibly already regretting the Vladimir Guerrero contract given both his regression and the recent work ethic concerns. As of now, he's the newest poster boy of why you don't give players contracts exceeding six or seven years.

"So should that scare Toronto into passing on Harper? Not necessarily. If the goal is to keep up with the other four AL East teams, and especially the Yankees and Rays, then Harper is worth the risk — so long as he's willing to play right field on the Rogers Centre turf."

If Harper does become available, many teams across Major League Baseball will be interested in his services. For Philadelphia, that could be a good thing. Ultimately, though, the return for a player of his caliber at this age won't be what it could have been a couple of years ago.

It's better if the Phillies keep him around and try to build another championship-level core, though that's going to be a lot more difficult than usual.

articles.title: Ranking MLB's Top 50 Rookies of 2026 Season
articles.summary: The 2026 MLB rookie class was loaded with top prospects breaking through in the big leagues, and likely featured at least a few franchise-level players, headlined by Detroit Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle.
articles.body:
The 2026 MLB rookie class was loaded with top prospects breaking through in the big leagues, and likely featured at least a few franchise-level players, headlined by Detroit Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle.

Others who shined down the stretch in 2025 but still carried rookie eligibility, including Sal Stewart, Nolan McLean, Trey Yesavage and Carter Jensen, settled in as impact players for their respective teams.

The other major storyline was Nippon Professional Baseball standouts Munetaka Murakami and Kazuma Okamoto immediately finding their power strokes stateside, each recording a 30-homer season.

Ahead, we've ranked the top 50 rookies of the 2026 campaign, focused solely on this year's production and not their future potential or long-term outlook. Offensive and defensive contributions were both taken into account, while a strong finish carried more weight than a strong start that ended in steady regression.

Stats: 64 G, 11 HLD, 3.66 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 94 K, 96.0 IP

Blubaugh finished third on the Astros' staff in innings pitched (96.0), despite working exclusively in relief. He recorded more than three outs in 35 of his 64 appearances, helping to prop up a shaky rotation.

Stats: 364 PA, 107 OPS+, .264/.322/.424, 31 XBH (10 HR), 3 SB

Lee saw regular action at second base (53 starts, 492.2 innings) and third base (32 starts, 270.0 innings) while providing an above-average bat. The Tigers have had success utilizing players like Zach McKinstry and Matt Vierling in recent years, and Lee fits a similar bat-first utility player mold.

Stats: 152 PA, 107 OPS+, .293/.353/.383, 8 XBH (0 HR), 10 SB

The Padres used nine different starting left fielders in 2026, ultimately settling into a productive platoon of Samad Taylor and Harris. After spending time with the White Sox and Astros earlier in the season, Harris hit .322/.364/.422 for a 120 OPS+ in 100 plate appearances after coming to San Diego.

47. C Brandon Valenzuela, Toronto Blue Jays

Stats: 271 PA, 89 OPS+, .226/.311/.377, 18 XBH (9 HR), 2 SB

An injury-plagued season for Alejandro Kirk opened the door for Valenzuela to start 68 games behind the plate for the Blue Jays. His offensive impact was limited, but he threw out 30.2 percent of base stealers and graded out as one of the best pitch-framers in baseball.

Stats: 289 PA, 105 OPS+, .245/.313/.429, 25 XBH (11 HR), 10 SB

With 105 strikeouts in 289 plate appearances, swing-and-miss remains a significant part of Jones' game, but he made enough of an impact when he did make contact to log a 105 OPS+ in 86 games. He had 17 extra-base hits, seven home runs and 28 RBI in 188 plate appearances over the final two months of the season.

Stats: 15 GS, 5-6, 3.42 ERA, 1.14 WHIP, 63 K, 84.1 IP

A fifth-round pick in 2023, Thornton had a breakout 2025 season in the minors (14 GS, 1.98 ERA, 0.81 WHIP, 78 K, 72.2 IP) and made his MLB debut in May. After a few spot starts, he became a full-time member of the rotation in July, logging a 3.28 ERA in 74 innings the rest of the way.

44. C/DH Samuel Basallo, Baltimore Orioles

Stats: 399 PA, 96 OPS+, .222/.291/.406, 29 XBH (18 HR), 0 SB

Basallo had a .772 OPS with 16 home runs and 46 RBI at the All-Star break, but he missed a month with right shoulder inflammation coming out of the break, and hit .154 with a .482 OPS in 88 plate appearances after he returned. Strong batted-ball metrics and the first-half production hinted at 30-homer upside if he can stay healthy.

Stats: 266 PA, 99 OPS+, .261/.321/.402, 20 XBH (6 HR), 9 SB

After a scorching start to the season in the minors, Ramírez played well in a part-time role on a contending Cubs team, seeing action at second base (34 starts, 312.1 innings) and third base (14 starts, 136.0 innings). An 18.4 percent strikeout rate highlighted advanced bat-to-ball skills in his age-22 season.

Stats: 206 PA, 114 OPS+, .272/.350/.417, 17 XBH (3 HR), 5 SB

Between his 114 OPS+ and strong defensive metrics (443.1 INN, 5 OAA), Clark delivered on the expectations that have painted him as Detroit's center fielder of the future since he was taken No. 3 overall in the 2023 draft. He showed enough after his July 31 debut to be the everyday guy heading into 2027.

Stats: 33 G, 19 GS, 7-5, 4.19 ERA, 1.32 WHIP, 125 K, 124.2 IP

Acquired along with Kyle Harrison in the deal that sent Caleb Durbin to the Red Sox, Drohan worked in a traditional relief role, served as a bulk reliever behind an opener and made 19 starts as a Swiss Army knife for the Milwaukee staff. His 3.73 FIP paints an even better picture of his effectiveness, and at 27 years old he fits the "late-bloomer" profile.

40. LHP Connelly Early, Boston Red Sox/Washington Nationals

Stats: 18 GS, 7-5, 3.33 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 94 K, 94.2 IP

The Red Sox made the surprising decision to flip Early in exchange for Curtis Mead at the trade deadline, and it looks like the Nationals got a long-term rotation piece out of the deal. The 24-year-old was injured at the time of the trade and only made one late-September appearance for the Nats.

Stats: 330 PA, 92 OPS+, .234/.282/.403, 23 XBH (14 HR), 0 SB

Mack led the majors by throwing out 26 base stealers, despite not making his MLB debut until May 4. He had back-to-back 20-homer seasons in the minors prior to 2026, so his 14 home runs in 105 games are not an outlier, and he should be the guy going forward after Liam Hicks was traded to Tampa Bay at the deadline.

38. LHP Robert Gasser, Milwaukee Brewers

Stats: 20 GS, 5-5, 3.87 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 103 K, 109.1 IP

After Tommy John surgery cost him significant chunks of the 2024 and 2025 seasons, Gasser returned to full strength this year and pitched his way into a prominent role on the Milwaukee staff. Over his final six starts of the regular season, he logged a 1.67 ERA in 32.1 innings, and the Brewers went 5-1 in those games.

Stats: 266 PA, 99 OPS+, .281/.350/.368, 13 XBH (3 HR), 19 SB

The Brewers signed Pratt to an eight-year, $50.75 million extension in April, and he made his MLB debut on June 16, pushing incumbent shortstop Joey Ortiz to third base. He hit .321/.380/.407 over his final 25 games to close out the regular season, and his glove was as advertised at shortstop.

36. OF/SS Cole Carrigg, Colorado Rockies

Stats: 372 PA, 112 OPS+, .279/.341/.477, 38 XBH (12 HR), 11 SB

Carrigg started his 2026 by serving as the starting shortstop for Team Israel in the World Baseball Classic, made his MLB debut on June 9 and ended the year as one of the most productive bats in the Colorado lineup. He hit .331/.379/.552 over 190 plate appearances at Coors Field, though his 112 OPS+ still represents strong overall production.

Players Who Were Worse Than You Think in 2026 ⚾

35. RHP Bradgley Rodríguez, San Diego Padres

Stats: 68 G, 17 HLD, 2.19 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 81 K, 74.0 IP

As if the Padres bullpen didn't have enough weapons, Rodríguez developed into a reliable high-leverage option over the course of his rookie campaign, finishing third on the team with 17 holds. He surrendered just a .212 opponents' batting average thanks to a fastball that averaged 98.3 mph and a changeup that generated a 39.9 percent whiff rate.

34. RHP Bubba Chandler, Pittsburgh Pirates

Stats: 30 GS, 8-10, 4.62 ERA, 1.40 WHIP, 140 K, 154.0 IP

Chandler finished fourth in innings pitched (154.0) and sixth in strikeouts among rookie pitchers, and he joined Parker Messick, Nolan McLean and Foster Griffin as the only rookie hurlers to make 30 starts. He took some lumps, but he is still only 24 years old and looks like a long-term rotation piece.

33. C/DH Eduardo Valencia, Detroit Tigers

Stats: 138 PA, 178 OPS+, .341/.380/.636, 22 XBH (8 HR), 0 SB

The No. 16 prospect in the Detroit farm system at the start of the year, Valencia was promoted to the majors in July after Jahmai Jones was designated for assignment. Among all players with at least 100 plate appearances in 2026, his 178 OPS+ trailed only Yordan Alvarez (190), though a .404 BABIP will prove difficult to sustain over extended action.

Stats: 181 PA, 129 OPS+, .329/.402/.424, 10 XBH (2 HR), 3 SB

The Blue Jays acquired Bateman in the deadline deal that sent Kevin Gausman to the Cubs, and he was immediately plugged in to replace Daulton Varsho in center field after he was moved in a separate trade. With a .402 on-base percentage and strong defensive metrics (6 DRS, 3 OAA), he settled in as the everyday leadoff hitter down the stretch.

31. SS Konnor Griffin, Pittsburgh Pirates

Stats: 339 PA, 98 OPS+, .272/.324/.404, 25 XBH (6 HR), 23 SB

Griffin was the second-youngest player to appear in a big league game in 2026, and while his rookie campaign was derailed by a pair of IL trips, he still tallied 2.1 WAR in 80 games. He will enter 2027 with some serious post-hype breakout potential after entering this year as one of the sport's most talked-about prospects.

Stats: 337 PA, 119 OPS+, .300/.373/.387, 19 XBH (3 HR), 8 SB

The Angels claimed Meckler off waivers from the Giants last January, and he was recalled from the minors on May 22 for his first big league action since a 20-game cup of coffee in 2023. The 26-year-old didn't provide much extra-base pop, but his .300 average and .373 on-base percentage made him one of the Angels' most productive bats.

29. RHP Trey Yesavage, Toronto Blue Jays

Stats: 20 GS, 5-6, 3.69 ERA, 1.14 WHIP, 97 K, 97.2 IP

Yesavage had a 3.58 ERA and 39 strikeouts in 27.2 innings last postseason while helping the Blue Jays reach Game 7 of the World Series, so he entered the year with more seasoning than the average rookie. A meniscus tear in his left knee cost him more than six weeks during the second half of the season, but he largely delivered on the hype when healthy.

28. LHP Brandyn Garcia, Arizona Diamondbacks

Stats: 57 G, 5 SV, 18 HLD, 1.93 ERA, 0.74 WHIP, 60 K, 51.1 IP

Garcia allowed just 27 hits in 51.1 innings while carrying a .155 opponents' batting average, which ranked right behind Mason Miller (.152 BAA) on the relief pitcher leaderboard. He allowed just three hits with his sweeper, limiting opposing hitters to a .054 average and 49.5 percent whiff rate with the pitch.

Ewing started 113 games in the outfield for the Mets, serving as a bright spot in a disappointing season alongside fellow rookie Carson Benge and superstar Juan Soto. He was a 3.1-WAR player on the strength of his defense (10 DRS, 6 OAA), and provided more than enough offense to warrant regular playing time.

26. OF Esmerlyn Valdez, Pittsburgh Pirates

Stats: 287 PA, 130 OPS+, .232/.345/.510, 32 XBH (17 HR), 0 SB

Valdez finished with 30 home runs in 128 games between Triple-A and the majors in 2026, and his elite batted-ball metrics suggest that level of power production could be sustainable over a full season in the big leagues. At the same time, his 37.6 percent strikeout rate will need to improve for him to reach his full offensive potential.

25. LHP Andrew Alvarez, Washington Nationals

Alvarez began the year looking more like organizational depth than a prospect on the rise, and he struggled to a 5.29 ERA in seven starts at Triple-A, but he ended up being one of baseball's most valuable rookie hurlers. In 17 starts, he had a 3.35 ERA, 1.29 WHIP and 86 strikeouts in 86 innings.

The Red Sox acquired Bennett in a one-for-one prospect swap with the Nationals that sent Luis Perales the other way, and he ended up being a key member of the starting rotation. His 4.6 percent walk rate was the third-lowest mark among pitchers who worked at least 100 innings, behind only Nick Martinez (3.6%) and Tarik Skubal (4.4%).

Essentially a non-factor during the first half of the season, Mesa hit .288/.338/.555 with 18 extra-base hits, nine home runs and 22 RBI in 158 plate appearances during the second half. His breakthrough has given what was a top-heavy Tampa Bay lineup another impact bat.

22. RHP Spencer Miles, Toronto Blue Jays

Stats: 49 G, 8 GS, 6-2, 4 HLD, 2.63 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 93 K, 95.2 IP

Miles did it all for the Blue Jays in 2026, starting eight games, working as a bulk reliever and pitching in some high-leverage spots late in games during the second half. His 95.2 innings were the fourth-highest total on the Toronto pitching staff, and his 2.65 FIP backed up his strong surface-level production.
