Armed with a fastball that averaged 97.3 mph and a wipeout slider that generated a 37.9 percent whiff rate, Fuentes was a major weapon out of the Atlanta bullpen, despite the fact that he just turned 21 years old in June. His 92-to-21 strikeout-to-walk ratio and .223 opponents' batting average speak to his advanced pitchability and dynamic stuff.

20. DH Bryce Eldridge, San Francisco Giants

Stats: 448 PA, 133 OPS+, .269/.364/.461, 40 XBH (17 HR), 1 SB

Eldridge entered the 2026 season with little left to prove in the minors, but also coming off a lackluster MLB debut when he hit .107 with 13 strikeouts in 37 plate appearances. He spent the first month of the season back at Triple-A, but eventually took over as San Francisco's primary DH, and his 23 doubles and 17 home runs are the tip of the iceberg on his power potential.

19. 2B Travis Bazzana, Cleveland Guardians

Stats: 517 PA, 110 OPS+, .245/.335/.408, 40 XBH (15 HR), 19 SB

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2024 draft, Bazzana played just 135 games in the minors before making his MLB debut on April 28. His advanced feel for hitting, extra-base pop and solid glove at second base helped him earn an All-Star selection, and he finished the year as one of Cleveland's most productive hitters.

Stats: 473 PA, 110 OPS+, .277/.359/.405, 29 XBH (11 HR), 21 SB

Injuries created an opportunity for Bolte in a crowded Athletics outfield, and he seized the opportunity with 3.3 WAR in 119 games. He played a terrific center field (909.0 INN, 5 DRS, 5 OAA), swiped 21 bases in 29 attempts and eventually served as the club's primary leadoff hitter.

Stats: 557 PA, 116 OPS+, .277/.370/.396, 37 XBH (8 HR), 20 SB

An impressive performance in the 2025 Arizona Fall League and a six-game run with Team Italy in the World Baseball Classic paved the way for Antonacci to debut in 2026. The 23-year-old had 133 hits, 43 walks and an AL-leading 29 hit by pitches en route to a .370 on-base percentage, and he spent the bulk of the season as Chicago's primary leadoff hitter.

16. LHP Foster Griffin, Washington Nationals/Cleveland Guardians

Stats: 31 GS, 15-6, 3.60 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 158 K, 172.2 IP

Signed to a one-year, $5.5 million deal during the offseason following a three-year run with the Yomiuri Giants in Japan, Griffin saw MLB action in 2020 and 2022, but not enough to exhaust his rookie status. The 31-year-old earned an All-Star nod on the strength of his plus command (6.2 BB%) and ability to induce soft contact.

Stats: 631 PA, 121 OPS+, .300/.390/.453, 49 XBH (16 HR), 0 SB

The Rockies acquired Rumfield from the Yankees in exchange for reliever Angel Chivilli, and he ended up staking a claim to their wide-open first base competition during spring training. His .390 on-base percentage topped the NL leaderboard, and he was one of only seven qualified hitters with a .300 batting average.

14. OF Chase DeLauter, Cleveland Guardians

Stats: 559 PA, 131 OPS+, .287/.363/.457, 49 XBH (16 HR), 11 SB

In a down year for star third baseman José Ramírez, DeLauter was the best hitter in the Cleveland lineup, and his 131 OPS+ narrowly edged out Munetaka Murakami (130) for the top spot among qualified rookies. He made 68 starts in right field and 58 starts at designated hitter, as Cleveland did a good job managing his workload after several injury-plagued seasons in the minors.

13. 2B JJ Wetherholt, St. Louis Cardinals

Stats: 619 PA, 102 OPS+, .242/.339/.365, 32 XBH (17 HR), 14 SB

Elite defensive metrics (13 DRS, 25 OAA) helped Wetherholt put together a 4.5-WAR season, which trailed only Brice Turang (7.3) and Brandon Lowe (5.4) among all second basemen. His bat cooled after the All-Star break, as he hit .210 with a .608 OPS during the second half, but his well-rounded game should make him a building block in St. Louis.

12. 3B Kazuma Okamoto, Toronto Blue Jays

Stats: 636 PA, 107 OPS+, .232/.310/.452, 59 XBH (33 HR), 1 SB

With 248 home runs and six 30-homer seasons during his 11 years in Nippon Professional Baseball, Okamoto was a well-established power threat, and he delivered in the first season of his four-year, $60 million deal. He also played better-than-expected defense at third base after some had projected him as a likely first baseman in MLB.

11. C/DH Carter Jensen, Kansas City Royals

Stats: 603 PA, 120 OPS+, .239/.323/.467, 64 XBH (27 HR), 2 SB

Jensen logged a 158 OPS+ with nine extra-base hits in 69 plate appearances as a September call-up in 2025, and he opened the season as Kansas City's primary designated hitter. His 64 extra-base hits led all rookies and tied for 15th-highest total in the majors, and he also ended up making 97 starts behind the plate.

10. RHP Walbert Ureña, Los Angeles Angels

Stats: 29 G, 27 GS, 9-11, 2.97 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 142 K, 148.1 IP

Ureña opened the season in the Angels' bullpen, making a pair of relief appearances before he was optioned to Triple-A, but he returned to join the starting rotation on April 19. From that point forward, he logged a 3.01 ERA with 140 strikeouts in 146.2 innings, and his 13 quality starts tied Payton Tolle for fourth-most among rookies.

9. RHP Logan Henderson, Milwaukee Brewers

Stats: 18 GS, 11-3, 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 110 K, 98.1 IP

Henderson began the year fighting for a spot in the Milwaukee rotation, and ended it as the clear No. 2 starter behind ace Jacob Misiorowski after posting a 2.32 ERA in 54.1 innings over the final two months. He did not allow more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts, and finished with a 110-to-19 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 98.1 innings.

8. 1B Munetaka Murakami, Chicago White Sox

Stats: 553 PA, 130 OPS+, .207/.347/.478, 52 XBH (35 HR), 1 SB

Ranked among the MLB leaders in average exit velocity ( 98th percentile ), barrel rate (100th percentile) and hard-hit rate (99th percentile), Murakami's prodigious power lived up to the hype. His middle-of-the-order production was a big reason for the White Sox turnaround, and he might have had a 40-homer debut if not for a hamstring strain that cost him 35 games.

Stats: 491 PA, 116 OPS+, .265/.337/.437, 47 XBH (12 HR), 8 SB

Acquired from the Rays for cash considerations in December, Peters was a surprise winner of an Opening Day roster spot, and he quickly played his way into the center field job that was vacated by the Luis Robert Jr. trade. He earned an All-Star selection, played standout defense and logged a 116 OPS+ in a 3.6-WAR campaign.

Stats: 700 PA, 117 OPS+, .263/.330/.457, 57 XBH (32 HR), 15 SB

Limited value with his glove and on the bases capped Stewart's WAR total, but there is simply no ignoring a 32-homer, 111-RBI campaign. He was the only rookie to play in all 162 games, and that grind eventually took a toll as he hit .247/.287/.280 with one home run in September.

Stats: 654 PA, 118 OPS+, .282/.346/.430, 45 XBH (20 HR), 22 SB

While more than a few rookies started hot before fading down the stretch, Benge hit .310/.373/.471 in 62 games after the All-Star break to solidify his status as one of the game's most promising young outfielders. He finished with the first 20/20 season by a rookie in Mets history, and his 4.3 WAR made him the team leader on a high-priced, star-studded roster.

Stats: 26 GS, 9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP

Tolle has a unique repertoire, with his four-seam fastball, sinker and cutter accounting for 87.9 percent of his pitch usage, but it proved effective in his first full season in the big leagues. After some ups and downs during the first half, he had a 2.92 ERA and 84 strikeouts in 64.2 innings after the All-Star break.

Stats: 31 GS, 12-10, 3.16 ERA, 1.17 WHIP, 194 K, 179.2 IP

After suiting up for Team USA in the World Baseball Classic, McLean pitched like an established veteran atop the Mets rotation, finishing tied for fifth in the majors with 20 quality starts. The 25-year-old had a 2.45 ERA in 84.1 innings over the final three months of the season, and should anchor the Mets' staff for years to come.

2. LHP Parker Messick, Cleveland Guardians

Stats: 32 GS, 12-9, 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 193 K, 186.1 IP

Messick burst onto the scene with a 2.72 ERA in 39.2 innings over seven starts in 2025, maintaining his rookie eligibility along the way. The 25-year-old entered spring training battling for a spot in the Cleveland rotation, and ended up being the best rookie pitcher in baseball, likely pitching his way to a top-10 finish in AL Cy Young voting and runner-up in the AL Rookie of the Year race.

Stats: 707 PA, 126 OPS+, .278/.376/.430, 51 XBH (18 HR), 12 SB

With 7.1 WAR in 156 games, McGonigle was surpassed by only Pete Crow-Armstrong (9.8), Cristopher Sánchez (8.1) and Brice Turang (7.3) among all players during the 2026 season. He also joined Steven Kwan and Geraldo Perdomo as the only players to rank among the 25 highest in walk rate and the 25 lowest in strikeout rate, while further bolstering his value with strong defense at shortstop and third base.

articles.title: Yankees on Wrong Side of MLB History With Rare Stat in Playoff Loss to Rays
articles.summary: The New York Yankees had a historically bad defensive performance in their 5-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday night.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees had a historically bad defensive performance in their 5-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday night.

According to OptaStats, the Yankees are the first team to have more different players record an error than a hit in a postseason game in 16 years:

The last team to earn that dubious distinction was the Cincinnati Reds when they were no-hit by Philadelphia Phillies ace Roy Halladay in Game 1 of the 2010 National League Division Series.

That marked only the second no-hitter in MLB playoff history, and since the Reds did not record a hit, it took only one error in the game for them to "achieve" the stat at hand.

As for the Yankees, they committed four errors on Monday night in one of the worst defensive efforts imaginable, and all four errors were made by a different player.

The Yanks also had four hits, but since Ben Rice had two of them, they had more players commit an error than get a hit.

Three of the errors occurred in the first inning and allowed the Rays to take an early lead, as third baseman Ryan McMahon flubbed a grounder and second baseman Jazz Chisholm threw the ball away on an attempted double play, which led to Yandy Díaz scoring the game's opening run.

The third error saw catcher Austin Wells commit catcher's interference, although no further damage was done after that.

New York's fourth and final error of the game came during Tampa's four-run fifth inning when shortstop George Lombard Jr. made a throwing error to first base, allowing Jonny DeLuca to reach safely.

A Richie Palacios single in the next at-bat plated the Rays' fourth and fifth runs of the night.

While errors were numerous for the Yankees on Monday, the only true source of offense was Rice, who crushed a pair of solo home runs in the loss.

After getting one-hit in Game 1 of the series, it can be argued that the Yankees were collectively just as bad in Game 2, putting the Rays in firm control of the series.

The ALDS now shifts to Yankee Stadium, though, for Game 3 and Game 4 if necessary, giving the Bronx Bombers a chance to get back in it in front of their home fans.

articles.title: Cam Schlittler Says Yankees 'Didn't Seem Like We Really Showed Up' After ALDS Game 2 Loss to Rays
articles.summary: New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler felt like something was missing during Monday's 5-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday.
articles.body:
New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler felt like something was missing during Monday's 5-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday.

Speaking to reporters after the game, Schlittler shouldered some of the blame in explaining it "didn't seem like we really showed up" to fall behind 0-2 in the series.

The issues started right out of the gate with the Yankees committing three errors in the bottom of the first, though Schlittler limited the damage to just one run.

The Yankees finished with four errors, tied for their second-most in 448 playoff games for the franchise. The fourth error on a bad throw by shortstop George Lombard Jr. was especially devastating.

There were two outs in the bottom of the fifth at the time, so the Yankees could have escaped only down 3-1. Richie Palacios singled immediately afterward to score two more runs to make it a four run deficit for New York.

Schlittler was charged with four runs, but only two earned in 4.1 innings. He also wasn't his usual dominant self with just two strikeouts, his fewest in a game since Game 4 of the 2025 ALDS against the Toronto Blue Jays.

In addition to the poor defense, New York's bats have been silent through the first 18 innings of the series. Ben Rice was the lone bright spot on Tuesday with two solo homers.

The rest of the Yankees' lineup finished 2-for-28 and they had one at-bat with a runner in scoring position. This came after they got one-hit in Game 1 on Saturday.

After making easy work of the Boston Red Sox in the wild-card round, the Yankees are now on the brink of being swept in a playoff series for the first time since the 2022 ALCS.

New York will get the next two games at home as it looks to keep its season alive. Game 3 between the Rays and Yankees in the Bronx will be played on Wednesday at 8 p.m. ET.

articles.title: Yankees' Errors Trolled With Taylor Swift Reference in Newspaper Headline After MLB Playoffs Loss
articles.summary: The New York Post didn't pull any punches Tuesday when it came to addressing the New York Yankees' error-filled loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday night.
articles.body:
The New York Post didn't pull any punches Tuesday when it came to addressing the New York Yankees' error-filled loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday night.

Tuesday's back-page headline read, "Errors Tour," which referenced the Yanks' many defensive mistakes, as well as pop star Taylor Swift's popular Eras Tour, which took place from 2023 to 2024:

In a 5-2 loss to the Rays on Monday, the Yankees had as many errors as hits with four each. Those errors led directly to three of the Rays' five runs.

Second baseman Jazz Chisholm's throwing error in the first inning allowed a run to score, and after shortstop George Lombard Jr.'s throwing error in the fifth, Rays second baseman Richie Palacios delivered a two-run single in the next at-bat.

The Yankees were shut out 1-0 in Game 1 of the ALDS, managing only one hit against Rays ace Drew Rasmussen.

New York was not much better offensively in Game 2 with only four hits, two of which were solo home runs by star slugger Ben Rice.

The defense was an even bigger issue for the Yanks in Game 2, though, as the Rays reached base and scored runs multiple times despite soft contact against Yankees ace and likely AL Cy Young Award winner Cam Schlittler.

Now, the Bronx Bombers' backs are against the wall, as they trail the ALDS 2-0 and are on the brink of elimination.

New York found itself in a similar situation in last year's ALDS against the Toronto Blue Jays, and although it won Game 3 at home to extend the series, it fell in Game 4.

The Yankees will look to do better this time around, but they will need victories in Games 3 and 4 at home in order to send the series back to St. Petersburg, Florida, for a decisive Game 5.

articles.title: Red Sox's Sonny Gray Reportedly Was Investigated by MLB Over Potential Use of Sticky Substance
articles.summary: Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Sonny Gray drew some attention on social media for appearing to have a sticky substance on his neck during last week's wild card loss to the New York Yankees.
articles.body:
Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Sonny Gray drew some attention on social media for appearing to have a sticky substance on his neck during last week's wild card loss to the New York Yankees.

However, Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com reported that MLB investigated the matter, and Gray "obviously passed in-game standard checks without penalty, which suggests he is in the clear." Cotillo added that "any discipline would likely have been levied by now anyway."

Regardless of whether Gray tried to use a sticky substance, it didn't help the Red Sox much as they suffered a 9-2 loss to get swept out of the playoffs. Gray lasted 4.2 innings and gave up two earned runs on six hits with five strikeouts.

After the game, Gray didn't address the substance on his neck, but he made it clear that he wasn't happy with being pulled from the game after throwing just 70 pitches.

"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that's a fact," Gray told reporters . "I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment. ... I felt good. I felt crisp. I felt sharp. I think I got clipped for a solo home run and then some singles, but I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I'm frustrated, for sure. You know, not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions."

On Monday, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy took the blame for his quick hooks of Payton Tolle in Game 1 and Gray in Game 2.

"The decisions are mine," Tracy said, per Ian Browne of MLB.com. "Not one time since I've been here has anybody scripted a game or has anybody told me to use this number right here to decide in this inning. Those decisions, they're mine. So, as far as that specific one [in Game 2 with Gray], that didn't, obviously, go great. That falls on me. Do we have data analytics? Of course we do. Everybody does. Is somebody standing there pushing me, saying you need to do this, this, and this? Absolutely not."

While Gray likely won't face punishment for the questionable substance, he will have to spend the entire offseason wondering what could have been if Tracy allowed him to finish off his playoff start against the Yankees.

articles.title: Yankees' Jazz Chisholm Jr. Talks Error in Video After Loss to Rays, 'I'd Probably Still Throw It'
articles.summary: New York Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. said, if given a chance to replay Monday's Game 2 of the ALDS, he would still attempt the throw that allowed the Tampa Bay Rays to score their first run of the game.
articles.body:
New York Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. said, if given a chance to replay Monday's Game 2 of the ALDS, he would still attempt the throw that allowed the Tampa Bay Rays to score their first run of the game.

"I'd probably still throw it honestly. The play that was trying to be made. I just feel like I could've probably tried to make an even better throw," Chisholm said Monday night.

Chisholm concluded, "I'd try and throw it a little more closer to the base. My back was turned, so."

Aaron Boone Calls Out Yankees Catcher 🗣️

Chisholm's throwing error took place in the bottom of the first inning Monday. Chisholm secured an out at second base before spinning and attempting to throw to first baseman Luis Garcia Jr for a double play.

The ball went wide, allowing Yandy Díaz to score the opening run of the game as the Yankees scrambled for the ball.

The Yankees went on to lose 5-2 and now face potential elimination in Wednesday night's Game 3.

Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters he didn't "necessarily have a problem" with Chisholm's decision to attempt the throw.

"Yeah, probably. Probably a little forced there," Boone said when asked after the game if he would have liked Chisholm not to attempt the play. "Obviously, you don't have great speed there, going down the line. So, yeah, probably best.

"If you're under control when you make the throw, though, it's probably gonna be bang, bang. So I don't necessarily have a problem with the throw. We've got to play catch. It's the big leagues."

Chisholm's missed throw was one of four errors committed by the Yankees Monday night.

Two others took place in the first inning, starting with third baseman Ryan McMahon bobbling a throw from Díaz and capped off by catcher's interference from Austin Wells.

That marked the most errors made by an MLB team in a single postseason inning since 1975, per MLB.com's Brian Murphy .

The Yankees recorded their fourth error of the night when a missed throw from shortstop George Lombard Jr. allowed the Rays to get a runner on base.

The Yankees were initially credited with committing a franchise postseason-record- tying five errors before one was taken off the board in the fifth inning, per SNY's Niki Lattarulo .

The club finished the game as the first MLB team in 16 years to record more errors than hits in a postseason game, per Opta Stats.

The Yankees' struggles took place after Wells made a costly baserunning mistake that caused him to get thrown out at third in the club's 1-0 Game 1 loss to the Rays.

Boone will hope his team can back Game 3 starter Max Fried with better decision-making as the Yankees play with the season on the line Wednesday night at 8 p.m. ET in the Bronx.

articles.title: From bidets to baseball magic: How Munetaka Murakami and his teammates revived the Chicago White Sox
articles.summary: It’s not much of an exaggeration to say that the Chicago White Sox used to stink. Enter Japanese slugger Munetaka Murakami.
articles.body: It’s not much of an exaggeration to say that the Chicago White Sox used to stink. After three disastrous years in which they’d lost at least 100 games every season, the South Siders had to freshen things up; but they couldn’t have imagined that some new toilet seats would be a part of the solution. Enter Japanese slugger Munetaka Murakami, who arrived in December on a $34 million contract, requesting that a few TOTO Washlet bidet seats be installed in the clubhouse. Since then, the Sox have really cleaned up their act, and are now on the verge of an American League Championship Series berth in the MLB playoffs with Mune leading both the charge and the celebrations. “I’m drunk!” he declared from the locker room after the Sox had clinched a wild card series win over the Houston Astros. Speaking without the aid of his trusted translator Kenzo Yagi, who was also celebrating with a beer next to him, Mune then bellowed a line that immediately went viral. “Yesterday, maybe hungover. “No, not yesterday, tomorrow. Sorry,” he laughed. “I don’t speak English!” At 6-feet-2-inches tall, Murakami is larger than life. He was nicknamed Murakami-sama in Japan because his feats at the plate were so God-like. He frequently launches home runs well over 400 feet, with an average exit velocity of almost 94 miles per hour that puts him near to the game’s elite. He emphatically announced his arrival in the Windy City with homers in his first three games – only the fourth player ever to start their MLB career so emphatically and the first to do so for the White Sox. Already an Olympic and World Baseball Classic champion with Japan, now the 26-year-old was showing the big leagues his raw power. He’d smashed 14 homers by the time he knocked his first double, an unusual record for a player starting their career in MLB. For now, his baseball was doing the talking, but those covering the team knew that he had much more to say. Brooke Fletcher, the team’s on-field reporter for Chicago Sports Network, describes Murakami as “sneaky funny.” “We always knew Mune had this sense of humor,” she told CNN Sports. “In spring training, you kind of get a feel for guys, but he didn’t show it much this season.” Fletcher says that Murakami was “locked in” for his rookie campaign. But every now and then, his quirky personality would peek through; there was the white sock that he pulled from his jacket at his introductory press conference, and the occasional one-liners that, due to their scarcity and because they were often delivered with almost comedic conviction, have become iconic. His bobblehead figure, distributed in July on a night featuring another two Murakami home runs, featured one of those lines: “I have power.” If you Google his name, another catchphrase – ONE HUNDRED – appears on the screen next to a champagne bottle emoji. When the White Sox clinched their first playoff berth since 2021 with a blowout of the Kansas City Royals, Fletcher was holding the microphone in an exuberant locker room. Asked to rate the celebration on a scale of one to 10, Murakami said, “100! No, 10. No, 100!” How many champagne bottles had he opened? “Hundred!” And finally, when asked to describe how it felt to celebrate with the team, he put his hand on the mic, looked into the camera, flashed a broad grin and screamed to a chorus of cheers from his teammates, “I am Japaneeeeese!” “When I did that interview with him and saw him like let loose like that, I was like, ‘Yes, like let’s go, finally!’” explained Fletcher. “Seeing the attention it got on social media, I was glad that people were seeing him for who he is. He’s a great guy in the clubhouse.” NBC Sports and Prime Video reporter Britney Eurton, who captured the “Yesterday, hungover” line thinks the reason that so many people are warming to Murakami is because his personality is so surprising. “Culturally, when you think about the Japanese, you might think they’re a little more reserved,” she told CNN Sports. “Shohei Ohtani is much more reserved and quiet, and I think Murakami is just more unexpected and that makes the energy through the roof. He’s a big dude, obviously, a big dude with a very big personality.” A magical turnaround Chicago’s success this season is far more than it could have expected when the Sox were eliminated from playoff contention last year on September 6. In 2023, they had lost 101 games, and things completely fell apart in 2024, when they were the worst team in all the majors with 121 losses, a modern-era record. Then only one team had a worse record than their 102 defeats in 2025. No team had ever made the playoffs after back-to-back 100-loss seasons, so to make it after three in a row was unthinkable, especially after one of their versatile pitchers was sidelined in spring training. Mike Vasil had been expected to carry a heavy load from the mound in 2026, but a torn ulnar collateral ligament in March changed everything. His season was over before it had begun, and yet he has still ended up playing a crucial role. It is unusual for injured players to travel, but Vasil’s teammates lobbied for him to remain in the dugout, and his involvement has helped the White Sox capture something magical. Back in April, reliever Jordan Leasure bought a $20 toy wand for Vasil to mess around with, and it has transformed the team’s fortunes. “It was in the locker room,” he told Chicago Sports Network, “and I decided to start ‘casting spells.’ The wand comes into play while we’re hitting because we want runs, there has been a couple of times when we’ve been pitching.” The month after the wand arrived, Chicago became one of the hottest teams in baseball. Murakami loved it. “Mune will sometimes ask for his own specific spell,” Vasil explained, with complete sincerity. “You could potentially catch it somewhere, but he loves his own specific kind of spell with the wand.” For example, after Murakami had homered against the Sox’s cross-town rival Cubs in May, the broadcast replayed a role-playing scene from the dugout moments beforehand, with Murakami intently following Vasil’s wand with his eyes and his body shuddering as he received “the spell.” Vasil now wears an embroidered wizard’s hat that was gifted by the fans and when team manager Will Venable told him the commissioner’s office had concerns about his wand, he appeared crestfallen. “What do I do now,” he said. “I don’t have an identity.” Venable, though, was joking. Everybody loved the wand, he said, and the White Sox subsequently handed out 20,000 replicas to their fans. Having now won their first playoff series since their World Series run in 2005 – and with a Papal blessing from Chicago’s own Pope Leo XIV adding some extra wind to their sails – the White Sox might be unstoppable. A 4-3 win over the Cleveland Guardians on Monday put them on the verge of the ALCS, holding a 2-0 lead in the best-of-five divisional series. It’s one of the most shocking turnaround stories in sports in recent memory – and they aren’t done yet. Their joy is infectious and other fans around the league are taking notice. They dance in the dugout before games, third baseman Miguel Vargas barks to celebrate homers and infielder Sam Antonacci dressed as Spider-Man to go to the movies. Whether it’s magic or chemistry or just good vibes, this team is having a blast. “These guys, they’re just playing a kids game,” Fletcher told CNN Sports. “They’re just having a great time.” Eurton concurs: “They feel like a group that just loves being together and playing together. I feel like they’re just a group of little kids out there playing their absolute favorite sport. Make no mistake, they know what’s at stake here, but they’re having fun doing it.” Nobody who’s seen them could deny that. And thanks to those new bidets and a cheeky bit of magic, it’s good clean fun to boot.

articles.title: Former Dodgers Executive Fred Claire Dies at 91, Helped Lead Team to 1988 World Series Title
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Dodgers announced that longtime executive Fred Claire died Monday, which was his 91st birthday.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers announced that longtime executive Fred Claire died Monday, which was his 91st birthday.

Claire was a member of the Dodgers' front office for over three decades, including serving as general manager from 1987 to 1998, and is best known as the architect of their 1988 World Series championship team.

Report: MLB Investigated Red Sox Pitcher

Per The Athletic's Patrick Mooney , Stan Kasten, the Dodgers' current president and CEO, described Claire as a "longtime key fixture of our organization."

"Fred brought many victories and Dodger legends to our franchise, as well as a 1988 World Series title," Kasten said in a statement. "We are forever grateful for his leadership during such a memorable era. Our hearts go out to his wife Sheryl and his family."

After working as a sports journalist in Southern California, Claire joined the Dodgers as a member of their public relations staff before rising to the role of GM. Under his leadership, the team developed its robust scouting and player development systems, which remain a hallmark of the franchise today.

Claire notably signed Kirk Gibson ahead of his 1988 National League MVP season, helping to pave the way for the team's World Series title that year. That title stood as the team's only championship for 32 years until it finally broke the drought in 2020.

Claire later made history when he helped Hideo Nomo become the first Japanese major leaguer to permanently relocate to the United States and join MLB. Nomo won the 1995 NL Rookie of the Year award with the Dodgers and helped create a path for future Japanese players, such as current Los Angeles stars Shohei Ohtani and Yoshinobu Yamamoto.

Claire's fingerprints still remain on the Dodgers to this day, and he will be remembered as one of the most influential figures in franchise history.

articles.title: MLB Legend Albert Pujols Talks World Series Pick, Cardinals, Manager Goals and More in B/R Interview
articles.summary: Albert Pujols' World Series pick is in trouble.
articles.body:
Albert Pujols' World Series pick is in trouble.

"They were playing the best baseball coming in for the last two or three weeks," the baseball legend told Bleacher Report ahead of the Division Series when picking the San Diego Padres to win the championship. "They remind me of my Cardinals in 2011, how we got into the Wild Card."

Believing the Padres would follow the 2011 St. Louis Cardinals' blueprint as a wild-card team to win the title made sense considering San Diego caught fire down the stretch and went 17-3 in its final 20 regular-season games to climb all the way to the No. 4 seed in the National League playoff picture.

That gave it home-field advantage in the Wild Card Series against the Chicago Cubs, and it took full advantage with two easy victories by a combined score of 12-1.

With Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado, Ty France and Jackson Merrill leading the offense and a shutdown bullpen featuring Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez to shorten games, the Padres seemed to have a championship formula.

"I think this is their year," Pujols said. "They started playing playoff baseball in the last three weeks to get into the postseason. Sometimes when you're hot like that, you just run through all the way. Machado and Tatis are swinging hot bats, and everybody in that lineup seems like they're inspired by Tatis."

However, the Milwaukee Brewers must have missed the memo, as they defeated the Padres in shocking fashion in each of the first two games of their Division Series.

It looked as if San Diego was going to take the lead in the ninth inning of Game 1 when France hit a towering fly ball to left field with a man on base that may have cleared the fence. Yet it ended up hitting the roof and falling harmlessly into Jackson Chourio's glove for an out.

Miller then gave up two runs in the bottom of the ninth to lose Game 2 in another stunning development, which means the Padres are staring at a 2-0 hole and have to turn things around at home starting Tuesday.

Perhaps they can, as Pujols explained the "postseason is about who is riding hot."

He would know better than most as one of the greatest players in baseball history with an astounding resume that features two World Series titles, three league MVPs, a Rookie of the Year, six Silver Sluggers, two Gold Gloves, a batting title, 11 All-Star nods and two seasons when he led the league in home runs.

His 703 career home runs rank fourth all-time behind only Barry Bonds, Hank Aaron and Babe Ruth, while Aaron (2,297) is the only player in history with more RBI than Pujols' 2,218.

Despite all those incredible individual achievements, his 2006 and 2011 World Series titles with the Cardinals stand out the most.

"This is what it's all about, playing for the postseason and to win a championship," Pujols said. "Yeah, it's great to make the money and all that, but at the end you want to be able to win a ring for yourself, your family and the fans. … There's nothing better than being able to raise the championship trophy at the end of the season. That's what you play for."

While Pujols played 10 years with the Los Angeles Angels and part of one season with the Los Angeles Dodgers, he is best known as a Cardinals legend with those two championships. All three of his MVPs, 469 of his home runs and 10 of his 11 All-Star nods also came with St. Louis.

He is all over the Cardinals' all-time leaderboard at second in home runs, second in RBI, seventh in batting average, fifth in on-base percentage, second in slugging percentage, sixth in games played, third in runs scored and fourth in hits, so it comes as no surprise he was inducted into the franchise's Hall of Fame alongside former teammate Yadier Molina in September.

"It was really an honor, especially to be going in with one of my brothers, Yadier Molina," Pujols said. "I never played for numbers. I've been playing baseball since I was six or seven years old, and I've been so blessed to be able to play for such a long time and to have an amazing career. These are the rewards that you get when you're done playing.

" … When I put that jacket on a couple weeks ago for the celebration, I thought of Lou Brock, Stan Musial, Bruce Sutter and Mike Shannon. Those were the guys when I got to St. Louis. I always looked forward to Opening Day to see those guys and to spend time with them. And now, knowing that I'm part of that legacy with those legends who were there before me, it was a pretty special moment."

With Hall of Fame players like him leading the way, the Cardinals were one of the gold standards of the league with eight playoff appearances in his 12 seasons with the team.

However, they haven't made the playoffs since he retired following the 2022 campaign.

That is an eternity in St. Louis, although Pujols and many other Cardinals fans found hope in a young core outperforming low expectations for extended stretches of the 2026 season as they look ahead toward the future with JJ Wetherholt, Jordan Walker and others.

"I love what the young players were able to do this year," he said. "There were no expectations, I think Oli Marmol did an unbelievable job of letting those young players play the game and play loose.

"I think they're going to be good for years to come with a really good core. Jordan Walker, Joshua Báez and JJ Wetherholt, I think they have that core, and if they add some pitching, they're going to be good not just for next year, but many years ahead."

Pujols is doing far more than just cheering on the Cardinals in retirement.

He recently partnered with Cologuard for their "Mind Your Behind" campaign in an effort to encourage screening for colorectal cancer (CRC) with the company's prescription-based, at-home test for adults who are 45 and older and at average risk.

The Cologuard Plus test detects 95 percent of colon cancers—the nation's No. 2 cancer-related killer—which is notable since 60 million people remain unscreened or are outdated when it comes to screening.

"I was excited when they reached out to me," Pujols said. "Especially when we talk about an issue like this with colon cancer. When you look at the number, 60 million people, on the screen, it's pretty crazy. To raise the awareness surrounding this is really important to me. I'm excited to be a part of it.

"To me, when I'm looking at those numbers and there's not much talk about it, that's what drove me into this campaign."

Leading by example is nothing new for Pujols, who began a managerial career following his playing days.

He started managing in the Dominican Winter League (LIDOM) during the 2024-25 winter season and led the Leones del Escogido to the league title and the Caribbean Series crown. From there, he managed the Dominican Republic in the World Baseball Classic and led the team to the semifinals before a loss to the United States.

And now he has his eyes on a major league role.

"I was able to explore that and was able to be the manager at the World Baseball Classic," Pujols said. "We didn't accomplish our goal, which was winning it, but I think 5-1 wasn't too bad. And we lost against one of the best teams in the tournament in the U.S. So now I'm just waiting to see if there's an opportunity to be with one of the teams. I would take that role and do my best to win a championship for that city."

Now it is up to a team to make the call.

articles.title: Anthony Rizzo, 2016 World Series champion, reveals most important piece to winning it all in MLB postseason
articles.summary: Anthony Rizzo revealed the unsung heroes behind the Chicago Cubs' 2016 World Series run, and why Gary Sanchez is one for the Milwaukee Brewers.
articles.body: With the MLB postseason in full swing, every team and its fan base vying for the World Series trophy is hoping that their superstars can rise to the occasion and get the job done. However, every great team who has hoisted the hardware at the end of a grueling season knows it takes more than just those All-Stars to win it all. In fact, it takes every single person from the top down. Just ask World Series champion and three-time All-Star first baseman Anthony Rizzo, who helped the Chicago Cubs break its 108-year streak without winning a World Series in 2016 after defeating the Cleveland Guardians in Game 7. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Of course, it was stars like himself, Kris Bryant and others celebrating on the field after he secured the final out at first base. But Rizzo can’t help stressing the importance of every player, coach, clubhouse attendant and more during October baseball. "I just think that on every team you have the stars, the middle-of-the-tier players, and your role players. Everyone’s so important to a team," Rizzo told OutKick, while highlighting PAYDAY’s "Low Key Legends" initiative, which emphasizes the importance of the unsung heroes within an organization. "It takes all 26 guys, it takes your entire staff. So, in order for the superstars to win their championship – let’s say Aaron Judge. He’s the MVP of the Yankees, of the whole league. For him to win a championship, it’s going to take every single guy on that roster. It’s not just one guy who carries you. "It’s the small things. It’s the baserunning, the pickoffs, the relays. It’s all the lowkey things that maybe don’t look as glitzy and glammy, but that’s what it takes to win a championship." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! We asked Rizzo who his "Low Key Legend" would be, and he didn’t even hesitate when thinking back to his career. "In the baseball world, I would definitely say Danny Mueller," he responded. "He was the clubhouse attendant in Chicago. He was my guy. He always had me high-energy, ready, and always a bundle of joy when I walked in. Whatever I needed, he was there. Then, the hitting coaches. They are just behind the scenes doing their scouting reports, knowing everything I’m thinking, so when I walk in, I don’t have to think. They just have everything ready for me, knowing what I want so I can go out there and play effortlessly. "Those are the guys behind the scenes that are just fueling this greatness you see on the field." At this stage of the season, teams have completely bonded into a family rather than just colleagues, if they didn’t do so during spring training and the early-season grind. Rizzo enjoyed every "family" he was a part of in the bigs, where October baseball brought out that team chemistry. "I think we’re together forever. We’re together for 200-plus days a year," he said. "In October, win or go home, you’re still saying to each other, ‘In a few weeks, I get to pick my own friends.’ So, we’re like family in the clubhouse. Guys know when to get on guys, when they need a little more love, when to back off – maybe they’re a little more sensitive. That’s the family and bond that’s created in a season. Every year is different. Every year is unique, but for me over my career, Danny’s been a low-key legend for me forever, and my hitting coaches I’ve always had a good relationship with them where they always had my dialed in." Then, when it’s time to play ball, it’s not just the clean-up hitter or the ace that carries the load of winning a postseason game. It takes a village, and the Milwaukee Brewers gave a prime example of that in Game 2 of their NLDS series against the San Diego Padres. YANKEES' JAZZ CHISHOLM JR MAKES WILD ADMISSION ABOUT COSTLY ERROR AS TEAM FACES POSTSEASON ELIMINATION Of course, the highlights will capture the moment Jackson Chourio walked it off in the bottom of the ninth inning with bases loaded and two outs against the Padres’ dominant closer, Mason Miller. That grabs the headlines and fan appreciation. However, Rizzo pointed to an unsung hero – a "Low Key Legend" – that helped make it all possible. "It’s a team of destiny because they’re a smaller market, but this is how they’ve been all year. To stay on brand with Payday and low-key legends, Gary Sanchez in the at-bat before, pinch hitting, taking the walk to get the bases loaded. That’s the low-key legend moment of the game. The superstar moment is when Jackson Chourio coming up and getting that base hit." articles.title: Dodgers Beat Braves as Yamamoto Shines, Box Score Stats, Highlights, Updated MLB Playoff Bracket
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Dodgers pulled back ahead in their NLDS matchup with the Atlanta Braves thanks to last season's World Series Most Valuable Player.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers pulled back ahead in their NLDS matchup with the Atlanta Braves thanks to last season's World Series Most Valuable Player.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto struck out 10 batters over seven innings to lead the Dodgers to a 3-1 victory. The Dodgers now lead the series 2-1.

Yamamoto outdueled Chris Sale in what was billed as one of the best pitching matchups of the postseason to date.

The 2025 World Series MVP barely flinched in the head-to-head showdown with Sale.

He fanned 10 batters over his seven-inning outing. He only conceded one run off four hits.

Atlanta's lone run came on a RBI groundout by Drake Baldwin in the bottom of the fifth.

By that point in the game, the Dodgers already had a multi-run advantage.

Enrique Hernandez and Freddie Freeman each homered in the top of the fourth in a rare bad inning for Atlanta's ace.

Hernandez's two-run shot from the No. 9 spot in the order opened the scoring.

Freeman, who almost hit a home run in his second at-bat, took Sale deep for Los Angeles' third run.

Sale hadn't conceded multiple home runs in a single game since July 4. He gave up two home runs over his last seven regular-season starts.

The Dodgers have an opportunity to close out the series on Wednesday night in Game 4. Tyler Glasnow heads to the mound for the Dodgers against Tyler Mahle for Atlanta.
